The German ambassador’s cipher telegram, cabled to Berlin for him by the State Department on 11 January 1917, holds 577 code groups. The first 147 are his telegram No. 205, whose German text he printed in 1920; aligned with the groups it fixes 82 groups of a two-part four-figure code, and a blind alignment test beats 2,000 shuffles and two control texts. The other 430 groups are a second text in the same code, probably on the peace note of 18 December 1916, and stay undecoded. 1166 · 0352 · 7031 · 1515 · 6147 · 9699 · 6699 Memorandum · Lansing · überreicht · . · Meines Erachtens · wird · Vorgehen 4879 Bruch · 7937 mit · 4873 Vereinigten Staaten · 2373 Wilson Washington → Berlin · two-part four-figure code · 10 January 1917 · key recovered from the printed text, partial Bernstorff to Berlin, 10 January 1917: the code telegram the State Department carried from Johann Heinrich von Bernstorff → to Arthur Zimmermann Go to the full text ↓ The German ambassador’s cipher telegram, cabled for him by the State Department, opens with his telegram No. 205, whose German text he printed in 1920; aligning the two recovers 82 code groups, while a second text of 430 groups stays undecoded. The State Department sent it on 11 January to its embassy in Berlin: “Please deliver following cipher to Foreign Office, from German Ambassador here”. Where National Archives (NARA), RG 59, State Department decimal file 763.72111/4443, microfilm M367 roll 166, frames 0785 and 0786 (naId 27179174). Catalogue entry 657. The cipher A two-part (randomised) code of four-figure groups; a five-figure group is a prefix figure on a four-figure base group. 577 groups in all, of which groups 0–146 are telegram No. 205 and groups 147–576 a second text. How it was deciphered Bernstorff printed the German text of No. 205 in 1920. Aligned with the groups, it fixes 82 code groups; every group that repeats does so where the printed word repeats, and a blind alignment test beats 2,000 shuffles and two control texts. What it says Bernstorff has handed Lansing the memorandum on armed merchant ships, and warns that acting on it will bring a break with the United States unless Berlin waits for agreement with Washington. Still open The second text (430 groups; 69 match known groups, no sentence can be built), the five head groups and the end group of No. 205, and five runs inside it whose split is not fixed. Credit Transcription, the identification of the ciphertext as telegram No. 205, the alignment and the controls by WAINUT (contributed 27 October 2026), done with AI language-model agents; a second agent re-checked about 117 groups on the full-resolution scans and redid the alignment with its own code. The plaintext is Bernstorff’s own print of 1920.
bernstorff1917.html#document

On 10 January 1917 Bernstorff handed the Secretary of State, Robert Lansing, a German memorandum on the armed merchant ships of the Entente, and asked the State Department to cable a cipher message to Berlin for him. Lansing’s letter of the same day (FRUS 1917, Supplement 1, doc. 75, filed as 763.72111/4443) at first refused, and names two subjects: “the new offensive armament of the merchant vessels of the Entente powers, and also my note of December 18 relative to peace terms”. A footnote adds that the message was sent the following day. It is the same State Department channel the Zimmermann telegram used five days later. The file holds the message as the State Department typed it for the cable: two sheets of figures, marked “1.” and “2.”, the second ending “DEPARTMENT OF STATE JAN 11 1917 APPROVED Robert Lansing”. Frames 0787–0789 are Lansing’s note and the “TELEGRAM SENT” form of 11 January; frames 0769–0775 and 0778–0784 are the memorandum in clear and its translation. Sheet 1, rows 1–13: telegram No. 205, from the head 958 677 728 229 0705 and 1166 0352 7031 (Memorandum Lansing überreicht) to its last group 0278 and the first group of the second text, 6497 . The clerk underlined the four-figure tail of several five-figure groups ( 54873 , 71621 , 11374 , 61166 ). Image: National Archives (NARA), RG 59 763.72111/4443, M367 roll 166 frame 0785, via catalog.archives.gov. The sheets carry 577 groups: 505 of four figures, 67 of five, 4 of three (the head) and 1 of six (group 377, 108609 , doubtful). The catalogue’s “about 150 groups” was too low, and frame 0786 is sheet 2, not a reversed image: the reversed figures in its margin show through from sheet 1. The typeface confuses 5, 6 and 8; on the full-resolution scans group 20 is 8918 and group 40 88789 . An independent re-reading of about 117 groups agreed on 116. The pencil tallies in the margin are a count for charging.
bernstorff1917.html#parts

Groups 0–146 are Bernstorff’s telegram No. 205. He printed its German text in Deutschland und Amerika (Berlin 1920), pp. 325–326, as “Ziffertelegramm, Washington, den 10. Januar 1917. Antwort auf Telegramm 148”; the English is in Official German Documents relating to the World War (Carnegie Endowment 1923), vol. II, p. 1017, no. 56, received in Berlin on 14 January. Neither print mentions the ciphertext or gives a code group. Groups 147–576 are a second text in the same code. It does not fit No. 205 (section 05). It is probably the part on the American note of 18 December 1916 on peace terms, the second subject in Lansing’s letter; that is not confirmed. The memorandum in clear on frames 0769–0775, which the catalogue suggested as a crib, is what No. 205 reports on, not its text.
bernstorff1917.html#code

Two-part code. The recovered groups follow no alphabetical order: aber 8335 , alles 4349 , Amerikaner 7294 , auf 8693 , bis 7424 , Bruch 4879 , Da 9793 , daß 8172 . Groups run 0000–9999 with leading zeros kept. Prefix figures. A five-figure group is a prefix figure plus a four-figure base group. In 21 of the 67 five-figure groups the last four figures also occur as a group on their own; chance gives about 2.2, and the first four figures do so in only 2. So 86699 vorgegangen ( 6699 Vorgehen), 88789 herbeigeführt ( 8789 herbeiführen), 11374 hiesigen Regierung ( 1374 hiesiger Regierung), 61166 des Memorandums ( 1166 Memorandum). Prefix 8 for a past participle rests on two cases; prefix 5 in 54873 (Vereinigten Staaten) has no known meaning. Several groups for the full stop. The eight sentence ends of No. 205 carry 1515 , 3377 , 0404 , 1515 , 3377 , 0404 , 1724 , 1515 . Which code. It is not code 13040, whose text of the Zimmermann telegram is mostly five-figure groups between 10000 and 24000. It is, by route and structure, the code Friedman and Mendelsohn (1938, p. 16 and n. 40) call 7500, also written 0075: they give the Bernstorff messages sent through the State Department as a two-part code of 10,000 phrases numbered 0000–9999. They name nine such telegrams, not this one, and no indicator is visible, so the attribution is a strong inference, not a proof.

The 82 base groups are in codebook.tsv , each with the positions that fix it and a grade (C: from the known plaintext and consistent at every occurrence; M: uncertain). 120 of the 147 groups of No. 205 have a value of their own. The passage below runs from “Hierzu muß aber jedenfalls” to “Davon abgesehen”: Hierzu muß aber jedenfalls [der] hiesigen Regierung Zeit gelassen werden. Da alles [7918] von Wilson entschieden wird, ist Besprechung mit Lansing reine Formsache. Er antwortet niemals, bis er Instruktionen von Wilson hat. Im vorliegenden Fall muß letzterer erst Denkschrift lesen. “For this, however, the government here must in any case be given time. Since everything is decided by Wilson, a discussion with Lansing is a mere formality. He never answers until he has instructions from Wilson. In the present case the latter must first read the memorandum.” Bernstorff warns that acting on the memorandum will wreck Wilson’s peace mediation and lead to a break with the United States unless Berlin waits for agreement in Washington, and suggests that Americans might be warned against serving on armed ships. Germany announced unrestricted U-boat warfare on 31 January 1917; the United States broke off relations on 3 February. The full German and English texts, with every hole marked, are given below under Full texts. Words in [?…] there come from the 1920 print and sit on runs of groups whose split is not fixed; they are not decoded from the groups.

Every code group that recurs in groups 0–146 recurs where the printed text repeats the word, and none is contradicted: 0352 Lansing (6, 84); 2373 Wilson (18, 78, 96, 112); 7937 mit (five times); 9699 wird (five times); 0197 von (77, 95, 118); 6918 7437 im Sinne (12, 141); 2396 2772 Friedensvermittlung (16, 113); 4879 7937 (5)4873 Bruch mit Vereinigten Staaten (24, 132), among others. A blind test that does not use the alignment maps cipher position p of groups 5–145 to word position p ·160/141 of the printed German (160 tokens). A repeated group scores when all its occurrences fall within ± w words of one shared word: window No. 205 against groups 5–145 control: No. 212 text control: No. 205 against part 2 blocks 2,000 shuffles (mean / max) ±6 23/25 8/25 7/19, 7/16, 8/16 0.43 / 0.76 ±3 20/25 4/25 3/19, 2/16, 5/16 0.17 / 0.44 ±2 16/25 2/25 0/19, 0/16, 3/16 0.10 / 0.32 No shuffle reached the observed score at any window (p < 0.0005). The No. 212 control is the opening of Bernstorff’s cipher telegram of 16 January 1917 from the same book. The letter-level statistical check ( docs/_validate.py ) returns “underdetermined”, as expected for a whole-word code with 1.38 tokens per type: swapping word values of equal length still yields German words, so the alignment test is the one that fits this code.
bernstorff1917.html#part2

Filling in the groups already fixed by No. 205 gives values to 69 of the 430 groups of the second text (16.0%), nearly all function words (ich, daß, hat, auf, für, Wilson, Friedens-). No sentence can be built and no plaintext is claimed. The second text opens 6497 8511 , and the same pair recurs at groups 277–278 (with 96497 and 98511 elsewhere), perhaps a heading or a formula. The run 8769 3865 2452 occurs twice (507–509, 512–514). A second pass on 2 November 2026 tried to read it and did not. Bernstorff’s cover letter ( FRUS 1917 Supp. 1, doc. 74 ) says the message refers to the armed ships “and to your note of December 18 last concerning peace terms”, so the subject is his own description. Friedman and Mendelsohn name nine sibling telegrams in Code 7500 with printed plain texts, each a possible crib, but no ciphertext of them turned up on 14 digitised reels, in the RG 59 OCR, or through the purport lists and name index. Catalogue entry 635, the crib named earlier, keeps no groups: the file copy (841.857/244) reads “(Quote German cipher)”, and the cipher was delivered to the Ambassador. An alignment against all of Bernstorff 1920 finds only No. 205 itself. On a two-part code one group gives no clue to another, so the other 361 groups cannot honestly be filled in from context, and no text is offered.
bernstorff1917.html#uncertain

Groups 147–576, the second text: 430 groups, 361 without a value. No printed or archival plaintext was found. A second pass on 2 November 2026 did not find a crib (section 06): the text is not in the prints, and no sibling ciphertext is on the digitised reels searched. What would serve is in archives: the Auswärtiges Amt draft, a Room 40 decrypt (TNA HW 7, ADM 137), or the sibling telegrams Friedman saw in State Department files. The head 958 677 728 229 0705 (probably “Antwort auf Telegramm 148”) and the end group 0278 (perhaps the signature): no value. Runs whose split is not fixed, with the words taken from the print, not decoded: groups 19–23 ( 0280 8918 8559 92312 5180 , “zum Scheitern bringen und statt dessen”), 28–30 ( 8584 0441 4171 , “wenn nicht mindestens so lange”), 59–63 ( 8951 73169 0358 0411 7599 , “welche zu Angriffszwecken bewaffnet sind”) and 125–131 ( 6436 0089 5051 5052 6011 1878 7325 , “muß ich pflichtgemäß bestimmt erklären, daß ich”). The last run contains none of the known groups for muß, ich or daß, so the cipher words it differently from the print or uses other forms. Grade M (uncertain): 1354 0321 “aus nicht ermessen” (split doubtful); 8096 unvermeidlich (doubtful reading of its figures); 0498 jedenfalls (der?); 06887 Instruktionen; 4118 vorliegenden; 1724 stop or paragraph; 71621 zu nehmen (placed by position only). 7918 at group 76 has no word in the print. Readings of the figures: group 447 is 28648 or 26648 ; group 377 108609 is doubtful; 06887 , 4118 and 0089 fit the glyph forms but are not certain. The novelty is qualified: no decipherment of this ciphertext and no group of this code were found in print, and the link between 763.72111/4443 and telegram No. 205 is not made in FRUS, Bernstorff or the Official German Documents. The search was light; Boghardt, The Zimmermann Telegram (2012), was not consulted.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. Telegram No. 205, Washington, 10 Jan 1917 (groups 0-146) read in part Bernstorff reports that he has handed Lansing the German memorandum on armed merchant ships, and warns that acting on it will wreck Wilson's peace mediation and bring a break with the United States unless Berlin waits until agreement is reached in Washington; since Wilson decides everything, he must first read the memorandum. Three weeks later Germany declared unrestricted U-boat warfare and the United States broke off relations. Builds coherent sentences, but under the read bar of 95% of words read as sense (79% here); the holes are marked in the reading. part 2 starts at 147 Reading reading_tel205.md # Telegram No. 205 (groups 0-146) as sentences, in German Bernstorff to the Auswärtiges Amt, Washington, 10 Jan 1917. Word division, punctuation and spelling follow the text Bernstorff printed in 1920 (Deutschland und Amerika, pp. 325-326), against which the groups were aligned. Marks: `[958]` = a group without a value; `[?words]` = words of the print that sit on a run of groups whose split is not fixed, or on a group whose figures are doubtful, so they are not read from the groups; `[der]` = a word of the print with no group of its own. The line-by-line decryption is in `decryption_tel205.txt`. ## Reading [958] [677] [728] [229] [0705] Memorandum Lansing überreicht. Meines Erachtens wird Vorgehen im Sinne dieses Memorandums Friedensvermittlung Wilsons [?zum Scheitern bringen und statt dessen] Bruch mit Vereinigten Staaten herbeiführen, [?wenn nicht mindestens so lange] mit Vorgehen gewartet wird, bis Einigung mit hiesiger Regierung herbeigeführt ist. Es wird sich vielleicht erreichen lassen, daß Amerikaner davor gewarnt werden, auf Schiffen Dienst zu nehmen, [?welche zu Angriffszwecken bewaffnet sind]. Hierzu muß aber jedenfalls [der] hiesigen Regierung Zeit gelassen werden. Da alles [7918] von Wilson entschieden wird, ist Besprechung mit Lansing reine Formsache. Er antwortet niemals, bis er Instruktionen von Wilson hat. Im vorliegenden Fall muß letzterer erst Denkschrift lesen. Wieviel Wert Euere Exzellenz auf Wilsons Friedensvermittlung legen, kann ich von hier [?aus nicht ermessen]. Davon abgesehen, [?muß ich pflichtgemäß bestimmt erklären, daß ich] Bruch mit Vereinigten Staaten für [?unvermeidlich] halte, wenn ohne weiteres im Sinne des Memorandums vorgegangen wird. II, p. 1017, no. 56. ## Reading [958] [677] [728] [229] [0705] Memorandum handed to Lansing. In my opinion, action along the lines of this memorandum will [?wreck] Wilson's peace mediation [?and instead] bring about a break with the United States, [?unless, at least for as long as it takes,] action is held back until agreement with the government here has been reached. It may perhaps be possible to have Americans warned against taking service on ships [?that are armed for purposes of attack]. For this, however, [the] government here must in any case be given time. Since everything [7918] is decided by Wilson, a discussion with Lansing is a mere formality. He never answers until he has instructions from Wilson. In the present case the latter must first read the memorandum. How much weight Your Excellency places on Wilson's peace mediation I [?cannot judge] from here. Apart from that, [?duty compels me to state positively that I] consider a break with the United States [?unavoidable] if action is taken along the lines of the memorandum without further ado. A letter of the Spanish ambassador in France to his colleague in London, in clear at the ends and cipher in the body. Brice Dudout rebuilt the key from the margin clears of the Duke of Feria’s letters to Coloma and read 375 of 425 cipher words (88.2%), but the key is only partly validated (two of four held-out tests partial, two failed) and about a third of the sentences read clean. Savoy, the Valtellina, a Lorraine garrison and Richelieu. so tt · R 57 fra z 96 · 20 · faz · + · 95 · faz tt fa en llegando a que (aquí) di quenta so = e · tt = n · fra = ga · 20 = a · faz = que Lyon → Carlos Coloma, London · syllabary on a grid with numbers and code words, in a clear letter · 8 December 1622 · key from adjacent plaintext, partial The Marquis of Mirabel to Carlos Coloma, Lyon, 8 December 1622 from Antonio Dávila y Zúñiga, Marquis of Mirabel → to Carlos Coloma Go to the full text ↓ The Spanish ambassador in France reports to his colleague in London on Savoy, the Valtellina and Richelieu; the key was rebuilt from contemporary margin clears and about 88% of the cipher words are read, with a weak validation. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 5 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial (88% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) · Daniel Bourdeau (pointer to a source) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial (88% of the cipher) The letter Antonio Dávila y Zúñiga, Marquis of Mirabel, Spanish ambassador in France, to Don Carlos Coloma, Spanish ambassador in London; Lyon, 8 December 1622. The opening and the close are in clear; the body, two leaves of it, is in cipher. The signature and a postscript are autograph. Where Biblioteca Nacional de España, RES/227/122 (Mss. 18.692), 2 leaves, on BNE Digital (CC BY 4.0). Catalogue 1601 here. No DECODE record, no entry at Cryptiana, no edition or study of the letter found. The cipher A syllabary on a grid ( fV = tV , xV = nV , cVr = rV and so on), two-digit numbers for letters and syllables, three-digit numbers and underlined tokens for code words, and a ligature for que . 969 tokens of 171 kinds. How it was read Brice Dudout rebuilt the key from the Spanish text written in the margin beside the cipher passages of the Duke of Feria’s letters to Coloma (RES/227/120–129), which use the same system, and tested it on passages held out in advance. The tests do not validate it : two of four measurements are partial and two failed. What it says Louis XIII’s proposals to the Duke of Savoy and the French answer; then Mirabel’s talk with the Queen Mother on the forts of the Valtellina and a Lorraine garrison, and a warning about Richelieu: he is not of the King’s Council “but it is he who governs the Queen Mother”. Still open 21 words unresolved, 29 restored from the sense alone, nine code words, three marked signs with no value. The reading is rough : by the repository’s sentence check only 52 of 148 sentences of the normalised text (35%) are clean. Credit Brice Dudout ( Europe chiffrée ), working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents: the transcription, the key, the tests and the reading, contributed by pull request #279. The margin clears of Feria’s letters are the contemporary decipherment the key was built on.
coloma1622.html#letter

Mirabel writes from Lyon to Carlos Coloma, the Spanish ambassador in London. The clear opening refers back to an earlier letter ( De Miñón os escribí a los 21 del pasado ) and promises an account of the proposals the King of France had made to the Duke of Savoy. The cipher carries the substance: the French proposals (restitution of the Valtellina, help in case of a rupture, the enterprise of Geneva), the answer given, and the Duke’s return home from Avignon. A second part reports Mirabel’s own talk with the Queen Mother about the deposit of the Valtellina forts, a Lorraine garrison and the capitulaciones de Aranjuez , and a short description of Richelieu. The letter is two leaves: f.1r has 25 lines, f.1v has 36. BNE Digital catalogues it as Carta cifrada . No decipherment is kept with it and no key is on its leaves. A scholarly edition may exist (M. Á. Guill Ortega’s biography of Coloma, 2007, was not read), and if it prints this letter or its key we will credit it. The top of f.1v, lines 1–7. The first line, so tt R 57 fra z 96 20 faz + 95 faz tt fa , reads en llegando a que (aquí) di quenta : so tt = en , R 57 fra z 96 = llegando , faz = que , faz tt fa = quenta . The underlined 204 on line 2 is the code word estado , 81 Δ is los . The passage is the one the reveal below deciphers. Image: Biblioteca Nacional de España, RES/227/122, f.1v ll. 1–7 (viewer image 6), via BNE Digital, CC BY 4.0.
coloma1622.html#cipher

Most of the text is written as syllables. A consonant sign changes its consonant by the vowel it carries: in this grid fV stands for tV , xV for nV , cVr for rV , xVr for sV , sVr for cV , sVn for pV , fVn for pVr , frV for gV and Vs for mV . Two-digit numbers stand for single letters and syllables, three-digit numbers and underlined numbers for whole words ( 309 negocio, 204 estado, _123_ Duque, 308 nuestro señor), and the ligatures faz , fez and fuz stand for que . Marked signs are different signs: a triangle is not a plain V, 94‡ is not 94, 20ʳ is not 20, as the clears of RES/227/128–129 show. Words are not divided. Three marked signs have no value: a barred 4 (4‡, in grande ), a q with an extra stroke below (in libre ) and an x with two dots below (in llegase ). They are in no key or clear available, so those three words stay restored. The same system is used in the Duke of Feria’s letters to Coloma (BNE RES/227/120–129) and in BNE MSS/18428 (Mirabel’s letters to Gondomar). The key is partial and is published as targets/coloma1622/key.tsv (CC BY 4.0).
coloma1622.html#key

Where the key comes from. The margin of the Duke of Feria’s letters to Coloma carries a contemporary clear beside each cipher passage. Brice Dudout and his agents aligned those clears with the cipher to deduce the grid and the syllabary, froze each key by SHA-256 before its test, and extended it from the clears of RES/227/128 and 129 and from Mirabel’s own letter. The last key frozen before a test is C04. The tests. Thresholds were fixed in advance: a key is validated at 0.85 of characters and at least 0.30 above the best of 200 shuffled keys; partial when the gap is at least 0.30 without the 0.85. Characters are aligned against the contemporary clear. test held-out passage score best control result C01 Mirabel f.1v ll. 12–21 (no clear) 0.333 0.169 failed C02 Feria, RES/227/127 f.1r 0.761 0.437 partial H3 Feria, RES/227/128 f.1v 0.690 0.419 failed (gap 0.271) H4 MSS/18428 p. 15 left — — no measurement H5 MSS/18428 p. 44 right 0.814 0.466 partial From targets/coloma1622/validation.txt . These are the contributor’s own pre-registered tests, not the project’s _validate.py . What that means. The key is partial by our protocol and not validated . Of four measurements, two are partial and two failed. A fifth reserve passage (H4) was burned without a measurement: its “margin clear” turned out to be the verso seen through the paper. That rule was fixed in advance, so H4 was not replaced that day. The first test (C01) was on lines of the target letter itself, measured with an earlier key and read with the later one. The key does well on the passages with a clear to measure against and has never reached the bar on one; the reading below rests on a key that fits those clears only in part.
coloma1622.html#reading

Every one of the 969 cipher tokens is covered in order by the word table of reading.md : 425 words, of which 338 are certain (values of the key, or a code word held by a contemporary clear), 37 probable, 29 restored from the sense alone and 21 unresolved. Certain and probable make 375 words, 88.2% ; with the restored words, 95.1%. Restored words are counted as holes, so the 95% bar is not reached and the letter is read in part. That figure counts words. The sentences are another matter. Counted as the repository does it (a sentence is clean with at most one hole in ten words), 52 of 148 sentences of the normalised reading are clean, 35% , and the check classes the text as not yet a reading by that test. Many sentences construe in Spanish, but most carry a restored or unresolved word, and several restorations correct a transcribed token from the sense. A blind sheet of 16 shape questions, answered by Brice Dudout, confirmed the transcribed token in eight of them and moved two words to probable. Read these sentences as a working text. The passage below is the stretch of f.1v in the snip, in the normalised text (unmarked = certain, {x} = probable, [x] = restored, ‹…› = unresolved). En llegando a que {aquí} di cuenta a la {Reina} madre del {estado} de los negocios, diciendo[la] que le corría {igual} [obligación] en desear y procurar que estas cosas se acomodasen en {buena} [correspondencia] de las dos coronas, pues en ambas tenía tales prendas, aseguróme ‹…› ‹…› que así lo ‹…›. Parecióme dar cuenta deste [Cardenal] de [Richelieu], que aunque no es del [Consejo] deste Rey, es por el que se gobierna la {Reina} madre On arriving I reported to the Queen Mother on the state of affairs, telling her that she had an equal [obligation] to wish and work for these matters to be settled in good [understanding] between the two crowns, since she had such pledges in both; she assured me […]. I thought fit to report on this [Cardinal] [Richelieu]: although he is not of this King’s [Council], it is he who governs the Queen Mother Savoy. The King of France has proposed to the Duke of Savoy the settlement and restitution of the Valtellina, the advantages of it for France and its allies, assistance if no settlement is reached, and help in case of a rupture as in the past; there was also a request for leave and assistance for the enterprise of Geneva (the reading restores who made it). The first proposal was answered that for the present France has other means for the Valtellina affair with the King of Spain, and the answer was put off to Lyon, where the Queen Mother would be told. The Duke went home from Avignon. The Queen Mother. Mirabel told her that she had an equal obligation to both crowns and describes Richelieu to her, and the answer, probably hers, objects to the Lorraine garrison as no matter of the capitulaciones de Aranjuez . Mirabel replied that the King of Spain had never doubted the Duke of Lorraine, but that France should also agree to the other points of the capitulations. The answer was that once the deposit of the forts was settled the rest would be; nothing on these points is settled until the King of Spain has been told. The end. The close, guarde os Dios como deseo, de León [Lyon], a 8 de diciembre 1622 , is in clear, signed by the Marquis. A historian will want the sentence on Richelieu first. It is read with a restored Cardenal (code 53), a restored Consejo (code 81) and the name written out in syllables; a scholar should treat the code words in it as inferred.

An intercepted newsletter from Brussels, printed in Birch’s Thurloe State Papers , in clear English except for a name of twelve digits and a word of four: someone “is come with a great train to visit the 0 9 3 7”. The crib “the king” fails on the name’s pattern and no key of the period fits. Not solved. 2 3 1 4 7 4 6 4 9 7 2 3 is come with a great train to visit the 0 9 3 7 key not found: a ten-digit cipher, sixteen signs Brussels → London · digit cipher · 12 August 1656 · attempted, not solved Brussels to Mr Copinger, 1656 An intercepted newsletter in clear English that hides only who has come “with a great train” and whom he visits; sixteen digits are too few to say. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained · On the map Credits · Thomas Birch (transcription) not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letter An unsigned newsletter, Brussels, 12 August 1656, “To Mr. Copinger, at the widow Andrews, in Bedford-bury in Covent-garden”. Intercepted by Thurloe’s office. Where The original is in the Bodleian, MS Rawlinson A vol. xli p. 78, not digitised. Printed by Thomas Birch, Thurloe State Papers (1742), vol. 5 p. 267. The cipher Single digits: a name of twelve (2 3 1 4 7 4 6 4 9 7 2 3) and a word of four (0 9 3 7), eight distinct digits in all. copinger1656.html#the-letter

The newsletter reports the Spanish siege of Valenciennes, the Swedish war in Poland and the Muscovites, and the fasting and processions that preceded the fighting. Then one sentence in figures: “2 3 1 4 7 4 6 4 9 7 2 3 is come with a great train to visit the 0 9 3 7. What his occasion is, is not yet known. God grant it be for good, for he is in a good way to gain his process.” Brussels in August 1656 suggests the arrival of Don Juan José of Austria as governor, or a visit to Charles II’s court at Bruges. The cipher sentence as Birch printed it, after the news of Valenciennes. Image: Thomas Birch, A Collection of the State Papers of John Thurloe (1742), vol. 5 p. 267, via the Internet Archive. This letter was one of four short pieces with no known decipherment in Birch’s volumes that Cryptiana lists together. They share only the printed source and each is in its own cipher: Beverning and Vande Perre to Boreel, 1653 , du Gard to White, 10 June 1656 and Waddall to “Vanyeare”, 22 August 1656 each have their own page.
copinger1656.html#tried

The name has the pattern ABCDEDFDGEAB and the word HGBE, sharing 9, 3 and 7 with it. If the word were “king” (“to visit the king”), its letters would force the name to read ?n?dgdfdig?n, which is impossible; so either the digits are not one letter each or the word is not “king”. Every royalist and Commonwealth key of 1653–60 that Cryptiana publishes was applied as well; none gives a name. Sixteen digits allow nothing further.

The name and the word (16 digits): not read. Blocker: too short. No key online; the ciphers of the royalist agents of 1656 would be in the Clarendon manuscripts, which are not online.

Powhatan Ellis (1790–1863), a former senator and judge from Mississippi, was sent to Mexico as chargé d’affaires in 1836, in the months after San Jacinto. He left at the end of the year, came back as minister in 1839, and wrote the passages that mattered in code. The catalogue entry (no. 653) came from a sweep of NARA’s scans that found pages of bare numbers with no words on them. Michael Brackx (issue #120) went through the three microfilm rolls. Coded pages, by despatch: vol. 7 (roll 8): 19 May 1836 (frames 0015–0019), 28 May (0025–0027), 25 June (0066–0067, 0071), 3 August (0123–0124), 7 September (0200), 24 September (0203–0204), a page with a pasted Cypher slip (0310–0311), 26 October (0323–0324); vol. 8 (roll 9): 30 November (0098–0099), 14 December (0208–0209), 21 December 1836 (0211); vol. 9 (roll 10): No. 9, 16 November 1839 (0298, 0299, 0302, 0303). He found the Department’s decipherments filmed with them: clean copies headed (Deciphered) or Cypher , clear copies, and clear text pencilled between the code lines. The 19 May clean copy is on frames 0020–0023, the 1839 copy on vol. 9 frames 0300–0301. Only 26 October 1836 has none on the film. Carlos Bosch García’s Documentos de la relación de México con los Estados Unidos III (UNAM, 1984) prints most of the 1836 despatches with the coded passages in clear, 26 October included.
ellis1839.html#the-code

Ellis used the code John Quincy Adams took to St Petersburg in 1809–11. Its table was rebuilt in this project from the clerk’s decodes and Ford’s printed decipherments of Adams’s despatches ( Adams at St Petersburg ). The same table reads Crawford’s Paris letter of 1813, Appleton’s of 1823 and Everett’s of 1825, so the Department kept this code in use for nearly thirty years. Applied unchanged, the table gives a value to 473 of the 519 groups of 1839 and 85 of the 90 groups of 26 October 1836. The rest are Ellis’s own usage. 1261 is a comma and 1264 a full stop; the table has no comma, and gives 1264 as gar . 401 is n (table: sian ), 1067 s , and 952–959 are the digits. Brackx fitted 97 such values on the 19 May passage. With them, the words recovered from the groups alone rise from 0.826 to 0.942 against the clerk’s copy. On the other passages the gain is small (0.815 to 0.833), so the values are largely specific to 19 May. They are kept as an overlay on the table, not as edits to it.
ellis1839.html#the-reading-1839

The text follows the groups, with the Department’s clear copy (frames 0300–0301) filling the groups the table lacks. The copy has “very respectable sources”, the groups “a most respectable source”; the copy’s misspelling “Toops” repeats the groups’ spelling. Since my despatch under date of the 14th instant, information has reached this capital, by express, that a body of Texian troops has crossed the line, and has been joined by a portion of disaffected Mexicans, with a view, it is thought, to attack Matamoros. I have not been able to ascertain the number of troops embodied for that purpose, rumour fixes it at between eight and fifteen hundred men, principally Mexicans. The government here is taking strong and prompt measures to meet this state of things, and will immediately put in motion, under General Arista, an army of four thousand men, to march to the frontier, there to act as circumstances may require. I cannot vouch for the correctness of these statements. They, however, come to me through a most respectable source, and are of sufficient importance to induce me to make them known to you as early as possible. A war with Texas under such circumstances will be decidedly popular with a large portion of the Mexican people, and I must believe unwise councils have influenced the public men of that country in projecting such a measure. The insurgents who were lately in arms against this government have either capitulated to the public authorities or have been dispersed by the force of the military, and in the event of an invasion like the one suggested, I am persuaded all parties will silence their personal and political animosities, in order to meet with undivided energy the common enemy. It is a favorite measure, I understand, of Mr. Cañedo, the Minister of Foreign Relations, to get up a general Congress of the independent Spanish American States, to consult, and provide for the general welfare of the whole. So far we learn, it is not likely to succeed. Arista left Mexico City for the north on 17 November 1839, the day after the despatch (Nance, After San Jacinto ).

Sir,"] Since my despatch under date of the 14th instant, information has reached this capital, by express, that a body of Texian troops has crossed the line, and has been joined by a portion of disaffected Mexicans, with a view, it is thought, to attack Matamoros. I have not been able to ascertain the number of troops embodied for that purpose, rumour fixes it at between eight and fifteen hundred men, principally Mexicans. The government here is taking strong and prompt measures to meet this state of things, and will immediately put in motion, under General Arista, an army of four thousand men, to march to the frontier, there to act as circumstances may require. I cannot vouch for the correctness of these statements. They, however, come to me through a most respectable source, and are of sufficient importance to induce me to make them known to you as early as possible. A war with Texas under such circumstances will be decidedly popular with a large portion of the Mexican people, and I must believe unwise councils have influenced the public men of that country in projecting such a measure. The insurgents who were lately in arms against this government have either capitulated to the public authorities or have been dispersed by the force of the military, and in the event of an invasion like the one suggested, I am persuaded all parties will silence their personal and political animosities, in order to meet with undivided energy the common enemy. It is a favorite measure, I understand, of Mr. Cañedo, the Minister of Foreign Relations, to get up a general Congress of the independent Spanish American States, to consult, and provide for the general welfare of the whole. So far we learn, it is not likely to succeed. [In clear on frame 0303: "I trust this communication will reach Vera Cruz in time for the New York Packet. I have the honor to be, with great respect, Your most ob. Serv. Powhatan Ellis."] Key: code_table.tsv

Three Latin letters between Ferdinand, King of Hungary and later Emperor, and the Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand in Brussels (Secrétairerie d’État allemande 540, DECODE R1887, R1889, R1890). The 1635 key was recovered from the Cardinal-Infante’s own draft, the 1640 syllabary from the ciphertext on top of it, and the different 1634 cipher from a clear phrase the letter repeats. 1635 and 1640 are deciphered in full; 1634 at 88.4% of its tokens. An independent re-solution: Andrew Aymeloglu published readings in September 2026. 04 10 h 8 m c 22 n · y p i f · 33 23 l 3 · z 37 34 15 32 p 34 ad hyberna vero quod attinet a = 0 n t z · e = 6 m p · 40–44 = la le li lo lu · pla–plu = ta–tu Stuttgart, Brussels, Vienna · homophonic alphabet with syllabary; vowel-series nomenclator · 1634–1640 · three keys recovered Ferdinand III and the Cardinal-Infante, 1634–1640 from Ferdinand III → to Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand Go to the full text ↓ Three cipher letters between the two Habsburg Ferdinands about winter quarters, Trier and money for troops: two deciphered in full with keys recovered here, the third largely. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 9 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method · 1635 letter: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext (complete) · 1640 letter: key recovered from ciphertext-only (complete) · 1634 letter: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext (partial) · On the map Credits · Andrew Aymeloglu (earlier solution, pointer to a source) adjacent text At a glance 1635 and 1640: complete (450 of 463 and 782 of 782 tokens) · 1634: partial, 88.4% of 474 tokens The letters Ferdinand, King of Hungary, to his cousin the Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand, Stuttgart, 28 October 1634; the Cardinal-Infante to the King, Brussels, 16 November 1635; Ferdinand III, now Emperor, to the Cardinal-Infante, Vienna, 22 February 1640. All in Latin, clear text with enciphered passages. Where Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État allemande 540. DECODE R1887, R1889 and R1890, all listed there as not decrypted; the Cardinal-Infante’s draft of the 1635 letter is DECODE R954. The cipher 1635: a Latin alphabet of numbers and letters, two to five signs per letter. 1640: the same alphabet plus syllables in AEIOU order. 1634: a different system of letter groups, numbers and drawn signs, also in vowel order. How it was done 1635: the draft, with the enciphered passages underlined, aligned word by word with the letter. 1640: the 1635 alphabet fixed, the syllables recovered from the ciphertext by annealing. 1634: transcribed here; its last cipher passage repeats the clear words that follow it, which fixed the first values. What it says The Cardinal-Infante refuses imperial winter quarters in Trier, a Spanish garrison town; five years later the Emperor asks him for centum mille florenos to be paid at Cologne. Still open In the 1634 letter, one word of six signs and a span of sixteen, each sign with a value but no Latin that fits; four conjectures on single signs. In 1640 one sign hidden at the page edge. Credit Andrew Aymeloglu published readings of all three letters on GitHub (aaymeloglu/unsolved-ciphers, 18–23 September 2026). This work found his repository on 30 September and did not open his key or text until after its own recovery. His README, which says the 1640 additions are mostly syllables, and his source list, which names the draft R954 (also on the DECODE record), were opened before the 1635 and 1640 work began. The two readings agree.

The two Ferdinands were cousins and brothers-in-law: Ferdinand of Habsburg, King of Hungary and Bohemia, succeeded his father as Emperor in 1637; the Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand, brother of Philip IV, governed the Spanish Netherlands from 1634 to his death in 1641. In September 1634 they had beaten the Swedes together at Nördlingen. Their Latin correspondence in the Brussels Secrétairerie d’État allemande includes three letters with passages in cipher, photographed on DECODE without a decipherment: DECODE Date From → to Cipher tokens Result R1887 28 Oct 1634, Stuttgart Ferdinand, King of Hungary → Cardinal-Infante 474 key recovered from an in-letter crib, 88.4% read as sense R1889 16 Nov 1635, Brussels Cardinal-Infante → King of Hungary 463 key recovered from the draft R954, complete R1890 22 Feb 1640, Vienna Emperor Ferdinand III → Cardinal-Infante 782 syllabary recovered from the ciphertext, complete DECODE has transcriptions of R1889 and R1890 (by “XZ”, January 2021) but none of R1887. The neighbouring records R1885–R1892 hold no key, and R1886 and R1888 do not exist. The R1889 record itself points to R954, the Cardinal-Infante’s draft of the same date. DECODE describes R954’s recipient as Emperor Ferdinand II; the letter addresses Serenissime Rex , so it is the King of Hungary. These are not the Ferdinand III letters of Klaus Schmeh’s Top 50 list (no. 27). Those are letters to his brother Archduke Leopold Wilhelm of 1640 and 1641, solved by Thomas Ernst in 2017 (“Zifra Piccolominea”). Ernst’s key does not fit the Brussels letters.

The draft R954: the passage to be enciphered is underlined in the text column ( Ad hyberna vero quod attinet … ); in the margin the secretary wrote the cipher and glossed it word by word ( hyberna , vero , quod , attinet , dicto , exercitu , caesareo ). Image: Archives générales du Royaume (Brussels), Secrétairerie d’État allemande 540, draft of 16 Nov 1635 p. 1, via DECODE R954. The draft gives the full Latin text in its right column, with the passages to be enciphered underlined. The secretary’s encipherment in the left margin carries a few glosses. That is plaintext beside the ciphertext. The letter’s 74 cipher words, 463 tokens, were aligned one by one with the underlined words. Where DECODE’s spacing ran signs together the image settled it: 04 10 is 0 4 ad + 10 , the h of hyberna ; 2000m is 20 c 0 m ( prae- ); 37731 is 37 7 31 . R1889 p. 1: the first cipher passage, Ad hyberna vero quod attinet … fieri desiderat , between clear words. Image: Archives générales du Royaume (Brussels), Secrétairerie d’État allemande 540, letter of 16 Nov 1635 p. 1, via DECODE R1889. A majority vote over the aligned pairs gives the alphabet (u/v and i/y one letter each): a b c d e f g h i l m n o p q r s t u x 0 n t z 8 9 7 x 3 4 6 m p 2 5 16 17 1 10 11 12 15 24 h 18 19 d e 22 32 a f l 20 g 30 33 c i q 25 26 31 34 37 23 35 38 y 39 Letters of the alphabet are cipher signs too, and doubled letters are written double. With this key 450 of the 463 tokens (97.2%) give the draft’s letter. The thirteen others are the copyist’s: 6 stands four times for m, 7 once for a and once for u, 9 once for p, 2 once for n; civitate lacks its it , prinncipis doubles an n, hctenus lacks an a. All of them are in words that the draft fixes. The enciphered passages, in the draft’s wording (clear words in brackets): Ad hyberna vero quod attinet, [quae Regia Dig.tas ac Dil.o vra] pro iam dicto exercitu Caesareo in Archiepiscopatu ac Civitate Treuirensi fieri desiderat. … Verum cum civitas Treuirensis iam inde a ducentis annis sub [Regiae suae Cat.cae Maiestatis] stet protectione atque [eo nomine] ab eius milite [semper quando id necessitas postulavit] fuerit praesidio munita, [uti etiam fuit cum] Gallus vexilla regia superans eandem occuparet; [Conveniens esse arbitror, ut] praesidium hoc regium in dicta civitate locisque circumiacentibus [conservetur, ex quibus] sumet alimenta necessaria [tum ad] sui ipsius uti convenit, tum principis electoris (cui hactenus ex aerario [Regiae suae Cat.cae Maiestatis] provisum fuit) sustentationem. … [quod] militi Caesareo in dictis locis difficulter hiberna concedi possint, [aeque boni laturam]. The King had asked for winter quarters for the imperial army in the archbishopric and city of Trier. The Cardinal-Infante answers that Trier has stood under Spanish protection for two hundred years and has had a Spanish garrison whenever needed, as when the French took it; the royal garrison should stay in the city and the places around it and draw its own upkeep and the Elector’s from them. He trusts the King will take it in good part that winter quarters there can hardly be granted.

R1890 p. 1: after the clear address, the cipher opens op fu 47 ap tis 34 | hi 41 x pli 21 47 | 23 m 25 34 c o m , co-mu-ni-ca-bi-t | di-le-c-ti-o-ni | u-e-s-t-r-a-e , Comunicabit Dilectioni Vestrae . Image: Archives générales du Royaume (Brussels), Secrétairerie d’État allemande 540, letter of 22 Feb 1640 p. 1, via DECODE R1890. The letter is enciphered almost throughout, 782 tokens. The first attack used nothing outside the ciphertext: a homophonic substitution solver (one sign = one letter, Latin 5-gram model plus a letter-frequency term), 76 restarts of 4 to 10 million steps. The same solver recovers a synthetic Latin text of the same length and symbol count (99.7% in 3 of 16 restarts), but on R1890 it never converged. So the letter is not a plain homophonic substitution. With the 1635 alphabet fixed, 424 of the 784 tokens have a value. The rest are numbers 14, 21, 36, 40–54 and letter groups such as pla ple pli plo plu , ap ep ip op up , tas tes tis tos tus . A free-value search pointed to 48 = no , 51 = re , 53 = ro : numbers in vowel order. The hypothesis was then one consonant per family and the vowels in AEIOU order, shown openly in the letter groups. All the best restarts of the family anneal converged on the same table: Signs Values Signs Values 40–44 la le li lo lu pla ple pli plo plu ta te ti to tu 45–49 na ne ni no nu ap ep ip op up ca ce ci co cu 50–54 ra re ri ro ru ca ce ci co cu ma me mi mo mu ha he hi ho hu da de di do du tas tes tis tos tus ba be bi bo bu an en in on un sa se si so su au eu ou uu pa pe po pu me mi mu fe fi fu at et it ot ga ge gi go ga gi ha hi 21 · 36 · b · o o · x · m · a The families ga gi = ha hi and at et it ot = ga ge gi go , and the single signs ko = do ( domus ), fu = mu , lx = oc ( occurrat ), li = xi ( existentium ) and 14 = tz ( Hatzfeldius , twice) were set from context; they are graded I below. DECODE’s uncertain readings were checked on the image: every “l/z?” is z (seven places), “c/1? o/0?” is the group co , “pla/u?” is plu . With these, every one of the 782 tokens has a value. The copy has three slips: igitua , materi , expredse . Comunicabit Dilectioni Vestrae orato[r] Serenissimi Regis Catolici marchio Castagneti ea quae circa novum apparatum militis in circulo Westphalico ab electore Coloniae et statibus illius circuli inceptum, ac quae inde in praeiudicium boni publici et etiam domus nostrae vereamur incommoda, secum fusius contulimus. Cum igitu[r] illud negotium celeri remedio indigeat, neque alius pro eo occurrat modus quam ut et nos festinanter collectionem militis, qui in potentiorem numerum quam dictus apparatus se extendat, in illis partibus instituamus, si alias liberam dispositionem ibidem servare et praecavere velimus ne ille circulus alieno arbitrio subiiciatur, ordinavimus eapropter quatenus comes Hatzfeldius se confestim Coloniam transferre atque huic operi qua maiore potest celeritate manum admovere debeat. Deficientibus vero nobis pro eo sumptibus necessariis, petimus a Dilectione Vestra denuo perinstanter quatenus iis quae sibi praedictus orator in hac materi[a] distinctius expositurus est omnimodam fidem habere et considerata rei gravitate desideratos hactenus centum mille florenos Coloniam custodiae nostrorum ibidem existentium commissariorum (quibus expre[s]se iniungimus ne quidquam ex illis praeter expressum mandatum nostrum aut comitis Hatzfeldii assignationem expendant) consignari curare velit. The Spanish ambassador, the marqués de Castañeda, will explain what the Emperor fears from the new armament begun by the Elector of Cologne and the estates of the Westphalian Circle. The only remedy is to raise a stronger force there at once, so that the Circle does not fall under another’s control, and Count Melchior von Hatzfeldt is to go to Cologne without delay. The Emperor lacks the money and asks again, urgently, for the 100,000 florins long requested, to be paid at Cologne into the keeping of his commissaries, who may spend nothing without his order or Hatzfeldt’s assignment.

R1887 had no transcription, so all 474 tokens were transcribed here from the photographs, line by line, with ad hoc labels for the drawn signs. Its system is not the 1635 one. It has three-letter groups in vowel series ( xar xer xir xur , tan…tun , pan…pun , for fer fir fur ), two-letter groups ( ob eb ib ub , ad ed id od ud , he hi ho hu ), numbers from 2 to 48, and drawn signs (a triangle, a slashed equals, struck m and D, crossed a and n, a female sign), some with superscript marks. A family anneal like the one used on R1890 collapsed to bare vowels. With consonants forced it gave Latin-like text that did not converge. R1887 p. 3: after posteritatem debetur gloria the cipher D/ m/ y ob 10 9 ten | o/ ≠ 2 K | he hi b ed xur 16 is followed in clear by the same words, promovere haud dedignetur . Image: Archives générales du Royaume (Brussels), Secrétairerie d’État allemande 540, letter of 28 Oct 1634 p. 3, via DECODE R1887. The opening came from the last page. The final cipher passage is followed by the clear words promovere haud dedignetur , and the three cipher words before them have exactly those lengths. Taking them as the plaintext fixes ob = mo , ten = re , he hi = de di , ed = ne , xur = tu and eleven single signs. That gives five families: ?b = m + vowel, t?n = r, h? = d, ?d = n, x?r = t. With those fixed, every top restart of the anneal agreed on the rest: f?r = c, ?c = vowel + s, ?r = f, l?s = g, t?s = s, p?n = l, s?l = b; the triangle = n, tt = s, 43 = in , 42 = en , and a superscript 9 doubles the sign under it ( 13^9 = ll ). Read word by word against the images, 324 tokens give the word directly, 95 need one sign read against its usual value with the word fixed by context, 26 rest on conjectures, 22 are open and 7 are terminal fillers: 88.4% of tokens read as sense , 93.9% with the conjectures. That is below the project’s 95% bar, so this letter is partial. Cum communis Augustissimae nostrae domus salutis stabiliendae ratio summopere requirat … facile colligere liceat ipsum nullos [ausus quos] restituendis illis, qui in fidem ac tutelam ipsius se coniecerint, principibus, imprimis Wirtenbergico et Durlacensi, profuturos esse crediderit, intermissurum. [Eventus] vero inde (…) non minoris emolumenti vel detrimenti rebus Dilectionis Vestrae quam meis [partibus] sit allaturus. Ideo cum quantum in me est subvertendis hisce communis nostrae domus hostium conatibus intendere non desinam, idem illud studium in Dil. Vestra excitare maximopere necessarium duxi. Eandem perbenevole rogans ut mediante aliquo, qui distractis illorum in diversas partes animis facilius mihi ad peragendum hunc ipsorumque (…) negotium armorum suorum motu et diversione, commune quod uterque praetendimus praedictae Augustissimae nostrae domus commodum, non minor [quam ea] quae ex conflictu Nordlingensi maximo suo merito ipsi apud Seren[issimum] … posteritatem debetur gloria, promovere haud dedignetur. Seven weeks after Nördlingen the King writes that the enemy will spare no attempt to restore the princes who have put themselves under his protection, above all Württemberg and Baden-Durlach. The outcome concerns the Cardinal-Infante’s affairs no less than his own, so he asks him to divide the enemy’s attention by a movement and diversion of his arms and so further their house’s common good, which will bring him glory no less than that owed to him for Nördlingen.

Andrew Aymeloglu published keys and readings of these letters on GitHub between 18 and 23 September 2026, and Satoshi Tomokiyo’s list of open ciphers marks the group “Two of Three Solved”. This project found his repository on 30 September and did not open it then. On 9 October, after the failed ciphertext-only attack on R1890, his README and source list were opened. So the 1640 syllabary was recovered by someone who knew it was mostly syllables, but no value was taken from him. For 1640 the two readings agree family for family, including the amendments l/z = z and c/1 o/0 = co . For 1634 both have the same families and the same open spans. This page adds suorum (he has quorum ), the conjectures ausus quos , eventus and quam ea where he leaves a gap, and confirms on the image the ib he marks as probable in intermissurum .

Where Nationaal Archief, The Hague, States General inv. no. 6894; DECODE R2113 and R2115, catalogued as ciphered with signs said to be zodiacal and alchemistic. The cipher A simple substitution whose signs are ordinary Latin letter shapes, with a numeric nomenclator of 116 entries in parentheses. How it was read The key sits in the same file and is on DECODE as R2118; it fits at once. The scans are bound out of order (R2115 runs p.3, p.2, p.4, p.1). Inventory number 6894 of the archive of the States General holds Haga’s ciphered despatches from Constantinople. DECODE catalogues four items from it: R2113 (1 February 1620, 3 pp.), R2114 (11 May 1620, 6 pp., marked Decrypted ), R2115 (4 May 1620, 4 pp.) and, as a key record, R2118, dated 1620 with the note that the date is fictitious and that the key was probably handed to Haga when he left The Hague. R2113 and R2115 were the catalogue target; R2114 was left alone, being marked Decrypted already. The key is two sheets. The first carries the alphabet table and the first part of the nomenclator, the second continues the numbered list to 116. The alphabet is a simple substitution in which the cipher signs are themselves letter shapes, so the ciphered words look like an odd Latin hand: The key, DECODE R2118: a–l. a is written φ, b K, c an 8-like sign, d ℓ, e 7, f o, g x, h 9, i an ε-like sign, k ω, l a looped 2. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, key sheet (alphabet a–l), via DECODE R2118. n–z: n is written like t, o as a cross, p as a u-like sign, q 6, r d, s z, t a long ʃ, u/v δ, w m, x B, y λ, z an n-like sign. The cell for m falls outside the photographed sheet. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, key sheet (alphabet n–z), via DECODE R2118. The nomenclator numbers the Sultan and his officers (1 Sultan Osman, 2 Sultan Mustafa his uncle, 3 the Vizier Azem, 4 the Capitan Bassa, 7 the Mufti, 10 the Janitsaraga), then the provincial Bassas and Beys, the cities of the empire, the Christian and Mahometan princes with their ambassadors, the fleets, and the islands and havens of both sides (93 Cyprus to 116 “de Golff”). Part of the nomenclator: 69 the Pope, 70 the King of Spain, 71 the Grand Duke of Tuscany, 73 the Grand Master of Malta, then the Turkish fleets and the islands. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, key sheet (nomenclator), via DECODE R2118.

Neither record is one letter, and neither is in order. R2113. Page 1 is the clear close of the despatch of 1 February 1620 and carries no cipher at all. Pages 3 and 2, in that order, are a different letter: page 3 breaks off in mid-sentence and page 2 takes it up, ending “In Constant. den xxxj martij 1620”. The opening page of that 31 March letter is not among the scans. R2115. The order is p.3 (which opens the letter of 24 April), p.4 (whose top ends it, “In Constantinopoli den xxiiij Aprilis 1620”, and whose foot begins the next), p.2, then p.1, dated “den [?vij] Meij 1620” (DECODE: 4 May; corrected on the full re-read of 23 October 2026, which also found that p.4 comes before p.2). So the record holds two despatches, of 24 April and [7?] May .
haga1620.html#march

The ciphered spans of the March letter run inside clear Dutch. On Transylvania, Haga reports that the Porte will let the resignation be made in favour of “sijn hoocheijts broeder”, and that the province must stay in good correspondence with Hungary so that it does not fall into the hands of Homonnai “ofte anderen {dependenten van t huijs van Oostenrijck}”. Then his own advice: Ick oordeel dat het {bij de turcken} meerder reputatie ende estime soude geven {dat de Ongaren regem Bohemiae mede erweelden, ende met} (62) in stricte alliantie verbonden bleven. Hungary and Bohemia united under one head, the Elector Palatine, would, he writes, let Transylvania deal with the Turks on better terms in the treaties that must follow; a legation from Hungary, Bohemia and the incorporated provinces would be welcome at the Porte. The second half of the letter turns to Spain. A Polish envoy has refused to have his lodging prepared in the usual way, which Haga calls a {bravade}; and (44) {ende} (45) {arbeiden bij} (4) om tyt te winnen, dat hy provisie {een suspensie van wapenen tusschen de turcken}, ende de {coninckrijcken van Napels} ende {Sicilia} gepractiseert mocht worden … (3) (4) {ende} (7) {vragen mijn} curieuselijck ende ernstelijck {off} (50) geresolveert sijn {de treffves met} (70) {te verlengen}, {vrede} te maecken, ofte {de wapenen} wederom {aen te nemen}, twelck men {hier seer gaerne} soude sien, {om Spangie van weder} zyde te mogen {infesteren}. That is the Grand Vizier, the Capitan Bassa and the Mufti asking the Dutch ambassador, in the last year of the Twelve Years’ Truce, whether the Republic means to renew it, and saying plainly that the Porte would rather it were broken, so that Spain could be attacked from both sides at once.
haga1620.html#april

The April despatch reports the arrival of the envoys of the confederated Bohemian and Hungarian lands, sent from the Easter diet of Pressburg with its resolutions and with the intention of sending a formal legation and making a perpetual peace with the Sultan. They were received without delay, by the Grand Vizier and then by the Sultan, and at that audience the ambassador of the Hungarian Estates (kept back until then, the letter says, by the persuasion of the ambassador of the German Emperor) was admitted with them. The Porte answered that the ambassadors would be welcome and that it was resolved to treat and make friendship with the crown of Hungary, Bohemia and the confederated lands. R2115 was transcribed in full from the four DECODE photographs on 23 October 2026 and every one of its 43 cipher spans decoded sign by sign with the key ( R2115_reading.md , with English; code words given as the key’s words, [?word] a doubtful word). The reading audit of 22 October had classed it decoded, not read, when only parts were transcribed. The advice: Daer is niet noodiger, als winninge van tijt, ende dat de Ungarische Stenden op het alderdesperaetste tot de electie ende croeninge van een nieu coninck procederen, daer naer [?hier] seer wert verlangt. Dat alreede aen [den Bassa van Buda] ordre gegeven is, met haer goede correspondentie te houden, ende, is noodich, te assisteren, sonder andere last van hier te becomen. Dat aen contrarie uijtstrooijinge, die van wegen [des Duytschen Keijsers Ambassadeur] souden mogen geschieden, geen geloof geven, [den opperste Vizir] ende [den Mufti] vermanen [den Prins van Transilvania], dat, sonder langer te wachten, de crone van Ungarie soude aennemen “Nothing is more necessary than to gain time, and that the Hungarian Estates proceed in all urgency to the election and crowning of a new king, which is much longed for here.” Orders have gone to the Bassa of Buda to keep correspondence with them and help them; nothing put about in the name of the German Emperor’s ambassador is to be believed; and the Grand Vizier and the Mufti exhort the Prince of Transylvania to take the crown of Hungary without waiting longer. Haga also reports that the letter of Bethlen Gábor to the Sultan, printed at Cologne by the Emperor to make the Prince odious, was never written. The closing pages are clear: the Polish ambassador has at last had his licence, the Khan of Tartary is said to have marched into Poland in person, and Ottoman preparations go on but will be slow, since neither Sultan nor Vizier goes in person.
haga1620.html#method

The DECODE JSON API gave the metadata for the whole run of records at inventory number 6894, which is how R2118 was found to be the key of the series and R2114 to be marked Decrypted. The fifteen page images were fetched with the account’s session cookie. They are photographed sideways, so every page was rotated and cut into strips of three lines before transcription. Mog. / oitmoedige dienaer [signature] ## Summary (modern English) **1 Feb 1620 (P1):** Haga reports that the Turks are pressing Poland: Poland must either pay a yearly tribute or go to open war with the Ottoman state. He also reports talks with the Emperor's ambassador about Hungarian fortresses, Turkish promises of help to Bethlen Gábor of Transylvania and to Hungary, and the Hungarian Estates' envoy. Nobody gets any real advantage from the Turks. **31 March 1620 (P3 then P2):** - On Transylvania and Bohemia, Haga reports: - the Porte would accept the resignation of Transylvania in favour of "his Highness's brother", meaning Bethlen's brother; - that province must stay in good correspondence with Hungary, so that it does not fall to Homonnai or other dependants of the House of Austria. Haga will watch this as far as he can. - In his view, the Turks would respect the anti-Habsburg side more if: - the Hungarians also elected the King of Bohemia and stayed in strict alliance with [62]; - Bethlen were compensated by other means for his great services and help to the crown. - This would strengthen Transylvania against all foreign powers and against the counter-mines at the Porte. - If Hungary and Bohemia were united under one wise head (the Elector Palatine), [62] could deal with the Turks in the coming treaties with more standing. - A legation from Hungary, Bohemia and the incorporated provinces would be welcome at the Porte. - A Polish envoy arrived but refused to have his lodging prepared in the customary way, which Haga calls a show of bravado against the Dutch side. - [44] and [45] are working with [4] to gain time and to arrange a suspension of arms between the Turks and the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily. Haga hopes these and other Spanish designs against the Christians will get no hearing. He believes they will not be granted. - [3] [4] and [7] ask him earnestly whether [50] has decided to extend the truce with [70] (the Twelve Years' Truce with Spain, due to end in 1621), to make peace, or to take up arms again. The Porte would gladly see the last, so as to attack Spain from both sides. ## Codes used [1] (twice, P3), [3], [4] (twice), [7], [44], [45], [50], [62] (twice), [70]. ## Signs that did not fit the key - **m = 4.** Confirmed by becomen (K78ϯ4 7t), met (47ʃ), mijn (4ɛɛt), vermogen, regem, cum. Words that were in cipher are not marked here; see `R2115_cipher_spans.tsv`. `[?word]` partly carried, `[…]` unread, `[15]`, `[46]` unidentified codes. ## Translation ### Letter of 24 April 1620 High and Mighty, Gracious Lords. On the [?16th] of this month two Bohemian and Hungarian [?commissioners] arrived here, sent from the Easter diet at Pressburg on behalf of the confederated lands, bringing letters and reports of all that was treated and decided at that diet, among other things that they intend to send a formal embassy to this Porte and to make a perpetual peace with His Imperial Majesty [the Sultan]. [?This] was so welcome that they [?enjoyed] a princely reception and quick introduction both to the Grand Vizier and to His Majesty, by whom not only these [?commissioners] but also the ambassador of the Estates of Hungary (whom the persuasion of the German Emperor's ambassador had kept back until now) had public audience on [?…]; and they will apparently be sent back in all diligence with full satisfaction and the answer that the ambassadors who are destined here will be welcome, and that the Porte is resolved to treat and make friendship with the Crown of Hungary, Bohemia and the confederated lands. Nothing is more necessary than to gain time, and that the Hungarian Estates proceed in all urgency to the election and crowning of a new king, which is much longed for [?here]. The agent of Transylvania showed me a [?certain] copy of a letter which Prince Bethlen Gábor is supposed to have written to the Turkish Emperor, which the German Emperor had printed at Cologne and spread throughout Christendom [?in order] to make [the Prince of Transylvania] odious everywhere. I have informed myself of it with certainty and found in truth that no such letter was ever written to the Turkish Emperor, nor were the sword, sceptre and banner mentioned in it sent from here to Prince Bethlen Gábor, before or after the Hungarian troubles; which I thought it useful that Your High Mightinesses and the other princes and estates (who have an interest in the preservation of the united lands) should know. By report of trustworthy and politic persons who lately passed through the Kingdom of Naples and pay [?good] attention to public affairs, [I am] told that the lands are so exhausted and ruined by the heavy burdens of the continual armament which the Viceroy has made against the Republic of Venice these [?some] [?years], that hardly any help for the German Emperor can be raised there. The Polish ambassador still stays inside, without leaving, apparently awaiting orders from his king. [?Herewith]. Constantinople, 24 April 1620. ### Letter of May 1620 High and Mighty, Gracious Lords. I find that the practices of the Imperialists to make peace between Spain and these lands [the United Provinces], so that the King might use all his forces by water and land unhindered against the Evangelical princes in the Empire, our United Netherlands and the Republic of Venice, will make no headway; to which end I have made such efforts and given such information everywhere that I have entirely disposed the [?Grand] Vizier (who before seemed to want to favour [the German Emperor's ambassador]) and all the [?chief lords] at this Porte in favour of the King of Bohemia, of [the Prince of Transylvania] and of [46], so that the ambassador of Hungary and the envoys mentioned in my last were dispatched in great haste on the first of this month, with their full satisfaction and letters from the Grand Signior, the Vizier, the Mufti, the Kahya and the Agha of the Janissaries to the said King, Kingdom and Estates, in particular that their ambassadors, whom they intend to send to this Porte, will be very welcome and agreeable; that the Porte is resolved to make a perpetual and firm peace with His Majesty of Bohemia, with him whom the Estates of Hungary shall [?elect] as their king, and with their confederated lands; acknowledging that the ambassadors may be dispatched to that [?end] without [?loss] of time, and that as long as they keep friendship with this Porte they need fear no enemies. That order has already been given to [the Pasha of Buda] to keep good correspondence with them and, if needed, to assist them without receiving any further charge from here. That no credence is to be given to contrary rumours which might be spread on behalf of [the German Emperor's ambassador]; [the Grand Vizier] and [the Mufti] urge [the Prince of Transylvania] to accept the crown of Hungary without waiting longer, since His Excellency, at my request, [said] he would work for it, that no peace be made with [the German Emperor's ambassador]. The honour of this resolution belongs to [Their High Mightinesses the States General] alone. [?With] the said ambassador of Hungary a chiaus has been sent to Prince Bethlen Gábor and the Estates to assure them by word of mouth of the aforesaid resolution and of His Imperial Majesty's good inclination, and [?to conduct] the ambassadors here and accompany them back. On the other hand, the dispatch of the chiaus and of [15] to [the German Emperor's ambassador] is put off from time to time, although they use great diligence to get an answer; but I hope that through our efforts it will come to nothing altogether, having well informed [the Grand Vizier] of the practices intended by it, to spoil the game in Germany and Hungary with such a bogeyman, against the intention of the Turkish Emperor and of His Excellency. The Polish ambassador has at last obtained licence to come here and be heard, having taken his first lodging with the Emperor's ambassador; but as the Cossacks again do great damage, tempers are embittered as before, and news is expected shortly that the King of Tartary has marched in person with all his power and fallen upon Poland. The preparations for war continue daily, although neither His Majesty nor the Vizier will go in person this summer, as they intend to do next year. The preparations at sea are made as usual. Herewith, High and Mighty, Gracious Lords, I pray the Almighty to bless Your High Mightinesses' prosperous and happy government more and more, commending myself most humbly to Your High Mightinesses' gracious protection. Constantinople, [?7] May 1620. Your High Mightinesses' most humble, faithful servant. Key: KEY_ALPHABET.md , KEY_NOMENCLATOR.md

The Paris volumes italien 1583–1593 belong to the Archivio Sforzesco, bought by the Bibliothèque impériale in 1867. Giuseppe Mazzatinti’s inventory ( Archivio storico lombardo X, 1883, p. 230) lists both slips under 1446: “f. 68. Risposta a quanto ha riferito Zorzo Maino (4 maggio). In cifre” and “f. 70. Lettera di Vincenzo Amidani a Fr. Sforza (Milano 4 maggio). In cifre.” That spring Sforza was under pressure in the Marche while Venice attacked the lands of Filippo Maria Visconti, duke of Milan; Sforza became duke himself in 1450. f. 68 carries its date in clear at the head, “M°cccc°xlvj die iiij° may”, and alternates cipher runs with clear Italian. f. 70 is all cipher, in another hand, and ends with a deciphered date line, “mediolani die qvarto mai” (Milan, 4 May), which agrees with Mazzatinti. The year and the Amidani attribution come from the archive; the signature after the date has not been deciphered. Neither slip has a known contemporary decipherment, and no edition was found. f. 68, the whole slip: the date in clear at the head, a cipher line, then two paragraphs in which cipher runs alternate with clear phrases. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, italien 1583 f. 68, via DECODE R7898.

it1583.html#method

Lasry transcribed the two slips in CTTS, which places a box on every sign: 839 boxes, of which 827 are cipher signs in 65 classes (425 on f. 68 in 52 classes, 402 on f. 70 in 48) and 12 are clear passages. CTTS generated the initial key from the ciphertext; Astra and Fable 5.1 then refined the key and the reading against the images and the context of both letters. The contribution’s verify.py re-checks every box, key value, edited segment and checksum, and passes. The key gives a value to 780 of the 827 signs (94.3%, four of them provisional). That is assignment, not sense. Counted here word by word, 721 signs (87.2%) fall in words that make Italian: 380 of 425 on f. 68 (89.4%) and 341 of 402 on f. 70 (84.8%). The difference is the isolated letters at the edges of unknown signs, the signature block of f. 70, and the untranslated se mono , do and da . The counting script is measure_sense.py in the folder. As a check against chance, the assigned values were scored with a Renaissance Italian language model ( docs/_validate.py , it-cinquecento, four-letter sequences): the decryption scores −2.07 per letter, two hundred random keys of the same shape average −3.76 (best −3.18), and a key fitted to the shuffled ciphertext reaches only −2.54. The test passes. Before this, the project’s own attempt of 21 September 2026 failed. It worked from a coarser draft transcription (404 and 390 signs, with diacritic variants merged), ran simulated annealing with the same language model under several constraints, tested word patterns, and checked all 208 Sforza keys on DECODE. Every run gave nonsense. That record, with the scripts, is in the folder.

General Joseph E. Johnston’s telegram to the Confederate Secretary of War during the siege of Vicksburg has five words in Vigenère. The War Department’s “Translation of Cypher” is filed with it, and the text was printed in 1864 and in the Official Records. The five words fit the Confederate key MANCHESTERBLUFF when the key advances by the length of each plaintext word, 26 of 33 positions, the rest being the clerk’s slips. June 16. 1863”) and image 3 a separate leaf, “Translation of Cypher”, with the note “words underscored in Cypher”. The telegram. The cipher words stand in the last three lines of the body: UNIEK – CXNKVNED, then JJTRRK, then ISLX – KFYHJEER. Image: National Archives, RG 109, naId 3854726, image 1, via the National Archives Catalog. The five cipher words are UNIEK, CXNKVNED, JJTRRK, ISLX and KFYHJEER, 31 letters. The catalogue had the fourth as ISDX; on the full-resolution page image its third letter is a script capital L, so ISLX. The second letter of KFYHJEER is a crossed “7”, the script F of this hand. The cipher lines: “will not this enable us to / UNIEK – CXNKVNED. for this / Genl Bragg & should JJTRRK – / Over ISLX – KFYHJEER –”. The War Department deciphered the words on receipt. Its leaf reads: “Will not this enable us to x invade Kentucky, for this Gen Bragg & should extend over East Tennessee”, with the five cipher words underlined and the note “x words underscored in Cypher”. The text was then printed twice: in Richmond in 1864, in Correspondence between the President and General Joseph E. Johnston … during the months of May, June and July, 1863 , and in the Official Records , Series I, vol. 24, part 1 (1889), p. 227, where it reads “the Ninth and Twenty-third Corps” and “General Bragg’s command should extend”. The letter to Bragg of 17 June (p. 196) quotes the sentence. “Translation of Cypher”, the Confederate War Department’s decipherment of 1863. The image is served at 1218 pixels wide, the largest the catalogue gives. Image: National Archives, RG 109, naId 3854726, image 3, via the National Archives Catalog.
johnston1863.html#key

MANCHESTERBLUFF is one of the Confederate Vigenère keys known from other messages, with COMPLETEVICTORY and COMERETRIBUTION. The catalogue entry had tried all three and found nothing. The reason is how the key moves: it runs on from one cipher word to the next, but advances by the length of each plaintext word. INVADE has six letters and UNIEK only five, so a key advanced by cipher length slips one place out of step from the second word on and matches 5 of 33 positions; restarting the key at each word matches 4. With the key advanced by plaintext length, the expected encipherment matches the written one at 26 of 33 positions: plaintext key expected written slip INVADE MANCHE UNICKI UNIEK key C used as E; last letter not written KENTUCKY STERBLUF CXRKVNED CXNKVNED the N left in clear EXTEND FMANCH JJTRPK JJTRRK key C used as E EAST ESTE ISLX ISLX none TENNESSEE RBLUFFMAN KFYHJXEER KFYHJEER one S (cipher X) left out The key was not assumed. Subtracting the 1863 words from the cipher letter by letter gives the key stream MANEH | STARBLUF | FMANEH | ESTE | RBLUFMAN, which is MANCHESTERBLUFF read straight through with the slips. Both places where the key letter is C were enciphered with E, so the clerk’s copy of the key, or his reading of it, had E for C: one systematic slip, not two. Controls ( check.py ): COMPLETEVICTORY matches 1 position of 33 and COMERETRIBUTION 3; 20,000 random 15-letter keys average 1.2, best 11; the fourteen wrong starting points of the right key give 0–4. Every other decryption is gibberish.

General Bragg informs me that a telegram from Louisville of the 10th says that part of the 9th, 23d Corps have been sent to reinforce Grant. Will not this enable us to INVADE KENTUCKY? For this General Bragg & should EXTEND over EAST TENNESSEE. J. E. Johnston, General. The cipher words are in capitals. Johnston, who had told Seddon the day before that he thought saving Vicksburg hopeless, passes on Bragg’s report that Burnside’s corps were going west to Grant, and proposes that Bragg use the opening to move into Kentucky with his command extended over East Tennessee. Only the operative words were enciphered; the movement of the Union corps went in clear. Vicksburg surrendered on 4 July.
johnston1863.html#uncertain

UNIEK: the fourth letter is an E with a hooked top. A hasty C would fit the key (27 of 33 instead of 26); either way the word is INVADE. The cross-like sign after “Bragg” is in clear, read as “&” on both the telegram and the 1863 leaf; the prints have “Bragg’s command”. Which telegraph office enciphered the words, and which copy of the key it held, is not shown on the leaf.
