A seventh record, R9236 (Add MS 4136 f. 140, catalogue 94), is another of Forbes’s leaves: the ciphered passages of Smith to Cecil of 15 October, 20 October and 15/17 December 1562, to the Queen of 4 November 1563, and of “Sir Thomas Smith’s advertisements from France, 31 Jan. 1562[/3]”. The clear words scattered through them (London, Lyn, Poole, Boston, Dover, Hastings, Garnesey) are the nulls of the same key, R9261; DECODE names R9262 as the nearest key, which is Throckmorton’s. Decryptions, added 21 September 2026: 15 October 1562 , all six passages: the Scots, the Queen of Scots, “to break with you, and to make war”, “that the hostages which you have shall be convoyed”, Flanders, Rollet and Monsieur Vyllemort. These agree with Forbes, Full View ii 119. 15/17 December 1562 , all six: “I see, you must hold ferme and fast: Frenchmen will come to reason but compellid … to trust no Frenchman of what religion soever he be … the Prince of Condé, which I do not believe … as soon as ever they be able, they will thither [bend] all their force”. These agree with Forbes ii 238. 4 November 1563 , to the Queen, decrypted in full and confirmed by the calendar (CSP Foreign vi no. 1366): “…de Montaigne … whose carte of La Rochelle … under another pretence. I have given letters to my Lord Robert and Mr Secretarie … from Rouen … wrote of that same matter … I thinke he can do. But this at this tyme is most necessarie.” 20 October 1562 , all four passages, with Forbes ii 122 as the check: [Newhaven] is not so strong as supposed; if it were summer they would attempt to afray our men thence “garden of chamillion upon the hill on this side”; things begun there by [France] be not perfit. 31 January 1562/3 , the advertisements: only passage (2), “the queen of Navarre”, is decrypted; (1), (3) and the last line remain fragments, and no printed text was found to check them against (not in Forbes, not in CSP Foreign vi): decoded, not read. One variant appears on this leaf only: a double bar stands for i . Passage-by-passage decryptions are in targets/smith1562/decipher_E.md .
smith1562.html#method

The six records and the Smith-series key records were fetched from DECODE. The first key record DECODE names, R9262, is Throckmorton’s third cipher. The record listing around it gave R9261, whose first page is Smith’s cipher and whose second is Sir James Croft’s. The passages were transcribed from the images and the key applied sign by sign. Forbes’s printed letters (vol. ii, from the archive.org text) and the calendar summaries were used only to confirm decryptions; where they did not fit the signs the passage was left open. Values added to the key: enos , listed at the top of the key among the nulls, is “Ambassador”; a marginal gloss on the 20 November letter spells it out. M̅ and M̈ are marriage and marry, B: is Bishop, C̄ is Congregation, J̣ is is or are, ! is in or into. The doubled long-s signs are st, the small open v is l, and a looped kite with a stem is w. A variant of the England sign stands for Earl (before Murray, Lennox and Warwick). The flag sign, the key’s “Germany” or “the Emperor”, stands where the calendar names Archduke Charles. Forbes’s copying slips: a single dot for a colon, 4 for e, ⊔ for π.

The hooked-T family of word signs (here, his, they, this, thing) is interpreted from context; Forbes’s dots on it are inconsistent (C). Undecrypted word signs: ẓ, ï, C·, F̄ and the ḧ-like sign in 1 September passage 2. Decoded, not read: 25 January 1564 and Avignon, 4 October 1564 (their contemporary decipherments are on the originals in TNA SP 70, “portions in cipher deciphered”, CSP Foreign vii 103, 714; State Papers Online was not reached), Narbonne, 7 January 1565, and the advertisements of 31 January 1563 (too short, no printed text). Single unread code signs, each seen once and not on the key sheet, in the letters of 1 September 1564, Marseilles 13 November 1564, Narbonne 7 January 1565, Toulouse 9 February 1565, 22 March 1566 and 29 April 1566 (about fifteen signs). The clear text of these letters (SP 70) is not in print; the calendar gives summaries only. Marseilles (5): the key’s sign for Calais where the calendar has Dieppe. Avignon passages 22–23 (“by litle and litle and by … great”) and 8–11 have no counterpart in the calendar summary (M).

Of what is done on that side ⟨we learn nothing except what they are pleased to spread abroad here.⟩ He should be someone who has some familiarity, acquaintance and credit with them; ⟨and⟩ I think Mr Middlemore would be a very ⟨suitable and fit man.⟩ As for help, if your Majesty does not intend to recall me, ⟨I have no doubt I shall manage well enough.⟩ ⟨I may be deceived, but by every means and source I can find, they intend⟩ to come to no agreement or settlement with your Majesty: ⟨they would rather⟩ agree to all the Admiral's demands. ⟨As for religion, they make no difficulty here in words.⟩ As for the offices, the Constable (Montmorency) ⟨will greatly help: he will begin, and already does, as men say, to⟩ suspect the greatness of the Duke of Guise and to weigh the ruin of the house of Châtillon, his nearest kin in France after his own children. ⟨Yet I think I see⟩ that if the Admiral holds out a while, or gives them another doubtful battle like the last (Dreux), ⟨necessity will force them to come to terms.⟩ ⟨What regard⟩ the Admiral and his followers will have for your Majesty ⟨I cannot say, having never met or known him;⟩ but if someone were with him from your Majesty as your minister, ⟨I think it would serve your Highness as well as anything could.⟩ ⟨Indeed, from all I can see or learn, it would be best for your Majesty to trust to your own strength, and so to provide that⟩ what you mean to do is done with all speed; In my miend, I had rather, both by water and land, we had made the profe of our furst strength and constancy there, as of a tast and essay, before they cam to Newhaven. I pray yow let me know, what opinion ye *have of that attempt whereof I wrote to the queen's majestie by Francis; I meane, whereof* I dowtid more of the possibilitie then the comoditie. In my mynde, it is not to be easely overslipped at this tyme, considering how things do stand even now. I have written also of *a thing now to the queen's majestie*, and in both my lettres, which is so necessary, that, after my phantasy, yt must not be let pas; *that is, to have one on the other side with the admirall: and I have named him who, for th'acquaintance with the admirall and all of that faction, the knowledge of the countrey, and all other respectes, is most fit. But you must dispach him streight, and owt of hand.* I pray yow, talke with Sir Nicholas, and beleve him and me in that. I am suer, when ye shall consider all, ye will well understand, and better then we, how necessary yt is, as this tyme doth shape and so longe as it doth thus stande; and the soner the better: nam dum in dubio est animus, paulo momento huc illuc impellitur. *You must not stic for honest allowance in tyme of service*, and specially such tyme; when, as I have written, ye may be ells servid as with a maske, except ye have one to se them at home in ther owen clothes. What tales so ever be told; what comfort, hope, despaier, or nedlesnes be laid unto yow; I do assure yow, there is nothing more necessary now, nor more likely to be necessary for this half yere at the lest, yf it be not a twelvemoneth or more, *howe long soever it be that France doth stand in those termes in which it doth now stand*. *Monsieur Danville*, as I here sith I came to Paris, *is to com over into England shortly*, with certeigne *agreements of the prince of Conde*. *It may well be answered: that* I have put up my demaunds in writing, *to the which the quene here* yet have made no aunswer; and whie should yow aunswer there, seing they will make me none here? and yf ye should, seing I am here *the queen's majestie's* ambassador, it weare reason, before yow should make any aunswer to that which they bring, that I should speake *with the prince of Conde himselfe furst*, and common with him aparte, to know whither yt be his hand and agreament ye or no *that they bringe; and whither, if it be his, it be not by compulsion and because he is a prisoner; and whither the prince of Conde* doth understand truly, what *the queen's majestie* hath done, *or I* her ambassador, in that matter and on his behalf. This or such like may be aunswerid, or as yow shall better devise then I. *But the truth is, this is but* a delay, and a tempting of you, *and to espie what power you have* ready, and a pretence owtwardly made to take occasion privilie and under hand to worke a ferther mischief: *for he shuld go from thence into Scotland* to kindle or set forward som new practize there, *to the detriment of England, and such noblemen of Scotland as favoreth the religion, and wold contynew the amytie between Scotland and us*: which bicause they can not bring to pas *that the Duke of Chattelrault do breake*, they are in such rage withall, that ye wold marvel at it: for they do not sticke som tyme openly to utter it. But as they here do by all meanes essay and go abowte it; so I do not dowte, but the quene's Majestie will and doth with all meanes provide, that there travail be in vaine. *He will ax a passport to go presently into Scotland: and* this is his errand in dede which I shew yow. *That once coming of Dehaye or Deese, th'Almaigne, belonging to monsieur Danvill into England* is suspectid to as many here as doth favour the religion, that it should be for no good. And altho' this had not chauncid (wherin I perceive, by the notes of th'examination, that his hede hath ben half a worker in the matter *of captain Mezy*) I had given yow warning of him at this tyme; I do here his often coming to and fro so much talkid on here of them who be ernest and curious *for the matter of religion. As for Danvile*; I do assure yow, he is taken here one of the most pervertid men, and one of the greatest enemies now to relligion. *The prince of Conde is now in his custodie*, as a man most suer against him. *As Sardigna* did corrupt *the king of Navarre, so th'admirallitie* hath cleane corruptid him: and therfore the Quene's Majeste must talke with him, as one whome *the Guisians do recon as* a man most suer to ther faction, *and they of the religion* do most abharre and suspect. This is now spreading, and they suspect here that⟩ the King of Spain and your Majesty are agreed, ⟨and that he would be content for you to make⟩ war on France ⟨to recover⟩ Calais, and more besides, ⟨if need be. I see nothing very different myself from my friendly talks⟩ with the Spanish Ambassador. ⟨However⟩ the French ⟨have agreed among themselves, I can learn nothing certain.⟩ ⟨I see that a great hold-up⟩ lies with the Admiral, who, as I understand, ⟨does not like the terms as well⟩ as the Prince (Condé) does, ⟨and holds out stoutly: he wants the King first to own the Prince's army and all its doings as done at the Queen Mother's command, and he wants⟩ your Majesty ⟨and their⟩ other allies in Germany ⟨satisfied of what⟩ was promised them. The Admiral is expected here post-haste with five ⟨or six horses; everything is said to wait⟩ on his coming. ⟨I pray God he⟩ acts wisely and is not trapped ⟨on the way or here. I cannot but distrust it as long⟩ as the Duke of Aumale and the Guise faction ⟨are so powerful⟩ around the Queen Mother, ⟨spreading such rumours⟩ about the Admiral, ⟨lest they have him⟩ killed, ⟨since they say⟩ he had the Duke of Guise killed. ⟨When I asked⟩ the Spanish Ambassador ⟨for news, having heard that the day before he had⟩ sat with the council in the camp ⟨— I tell him in jest that he⟩ governs the whole council of France — ⟨he told me nothing, saying they were so dismayed by the news⟩ of the surrender of the castle of Caen ⟨that they did not know what to do. He kept asking me whether⟩ the English held it entirely ⟨or were at least able⟩ to master the French. ⟨"Well," he said,⟩ "if you are masters there, ⟨I dare give you⟩ Calais, and ⟨three hundred⟩ of the ⟨five hundred⟩ thousand crowns ⟨you⟩ claim as the forfeit, rather ⟨than have you keep that⟩ castle, Dieppe and Newhaven (Le Havre); ⟨and if you⟩ keep ⟨them, your⟩ peace is made, if the Queen wishes, ⟨and all your⟩ requests granted." ⟨But he does not think⟩ the Admiral or any other Frenchman is to be trusted, ⟨and he would by all means have⟩ the English in all three places ⟨alone, or at least⟩ able to master all the rest at all times. ⟨I send your Majesty⟩ letters from Orléans ⟨by which you will see⟩ the state of affairs here. ⟨They have won over⟩ the Prince of Condé, ⟨and I know he has promised that,⟩ if his demands are granted, ⟨he will be among the first,⟩ after one or two summonses, to help drive your forces out of France. ⟨I have also had letters from⟩ the Admiral and Sir Nicholas (Throckmorton) at Caen. Those from Orléans ⟨I think the most important. I have⟩ lost one of my men there. Orléans is kept as strictly now, in this truce, as ever. ⟨The rest from⟩ Caen ⟨was of no great matter, except the surrender⟩ of Bayeux and Falaise. ⟨If⟩ the Admiral ⟨is no more trustworthy⟩ than the Prince, ⟨I expect all the war⟩ will be turned there. ⟨From⟩ the Emperor's messenger, Monsieur Achilles, ⟨I gather that⟩ the French King ⟨will not give up⟩ Metz, Toul and Verdun, ⟨and in that case⟩ the Emperor will declare war. But if the Admiral holds out and stays loyal, all will be well. No. 05, Smith to Cecil, 13 Apr 1563 (R9250, f. 159) Smith to Cecil, Amboise, 13 Apr 1563 (Forbes ii 384-386): Condé, sworn in his authority, is thought a new King of Navarre, won by the papists; to deal with the Admiral or d'Andelot is vain, all must be done with the Queen Mother and the Prince; the Spanish ambassador says Philip will not meddle in a quarrel between England and France over Calais or Newhaven; Smith would take Calais. The Ambassador of Spain ⟨tellith me allwais,⟩ that the King of Spain, so long ⟨as the quarrell was for obedience, and rebellion to the King of Fraunce, or for religion, was readie to helpe: but when it comith to be a quarrell of the crowne, or of the territorie of⟩ England and France, as Calais or Newhaven, ⟨he assureth me, he will not medle, nor will breake the old league⟩ of Englande ⟨for any new alliance.⟩ ⟨Yf ther weare no wiser than I, I wold not now demaunde, but⟩ take Calais. The Spanish Ambassador ⟨always tells me⟩ that the King of Spain, as long ⟨as the quarrel was about obedience and rebellion against the King of France, or about religion, was ready to help; but when it becomes a quarrel over the crown, or over the territory of⟩ England and France, such as Calais or Newhaven (Le Havre), ⟨he assures me he will not meddle, nor break the old league⟩ with England ⟨for any new alliance.⟩ ⟨If no one were wiser than I, I would not now demand, but⟩ take Calais. No passage contradicts the calendar, and no crib was forced. The last lines are tentative and not in CSP. - **Arles 22 Nov (CSP 808):** 2 short passages, read only in part (the Archduke Charles sign; marriage with the Queen's Majesty [?]). - **Arles 24 Nov (CSP 815):** the whole 12-line block is read except a few code signs. - **Narbonne 7 Jan 1565 (CSP 916):** read in large part. - **Toulouse 9 Feb 1565 (CSP 979):** 10 of 10 read, and 1 only in part. - Every reading was made from the glyphs and then checked against CSP. No passage contradicts the calendar, and no crib was forced. The unread items are code signs that are not in the key as read: ⟨J̣⟩, ⟨ẓ⟩, ⟨ï⟩, ⟨C·⟩, ⟨F̄⟩, the (2) sign of 1 Sep, and Marseilles (3) and (10). - Key additions: Enos = Ambassador (a code word, not a null); m̄/M̈ = marriage/marry; :F = French; the flag sign is probably the Emperor's house / Archduke Charles; the kite ξ = w and the plain ξ = d. It is probably the key's "the Emperor" sign, used for the Emperor's house. - **B: = bishop** and **:L = Lord**, as in the key. Smolensk was besieged by the Muscovite army of Mikhail Shein from October 1632 until Władysław IV relieved it in September 1633. Krzysztof Radziwiłł, field hetman of Lithuania, lay with the Lithuanian army near Krasne, and the garrison sent him messengers through the siege lines. Mirosław Nagielski printed five ciphered letters of the deputy governor Samuel Sokoliński from 31 May to 30 June 1633, which reached the hetman together on 4 July. This letter, dated 1 June 1633, is not among them: it comes from the officials and citizens of the palatinate, and the clear close on f. 2 carries about seventeen signatures. The unit, AGAD Archiwum Radziwiłłów dz. II nr 1116, has two leaves on microfilm. F. 1r holds the clear heading 1633 Junii 1 and salutation, then 35 lines of cipher. F. 2r holds two more lines of cipher, then the clear close and the signatures. There is no decipherment between the lines or on the address leaf. F. 1r, lines 1–3: Za gwałtownym i potężnym a barzo ścisłym opasaniem straża murów smoleńskich przez nieprzyiaciela wysyłać do W.X.M. rzecz barzo trudna… Image: Archiwum Główne Akt Dawnych, Warsaw, Archiwum Radziwiłłów dz. II nr 1116 f. 1r, via szukajwarchiwach.gov.pl.

Each letter has one sign, and the words are spaced as in clear. The signs are digits, and what tells them apart is the cross stroke. A plain 7 is g , a 7 with a small cross on its top is m , and a z-shaped 7 struck through is p . A free cross with a foot is z , and a plain free cross is s . The three groups of 1 and 0 are three letters: ŧ0 is w , +0 is u , and a plain 10 is k . A delta sign stands for the X of W.X.Mci (Waszey Xiążęcey Mości, Your Princely Grace). letter sign letter sign letter sign a 9 i, y, j 4 r 6 with a top flag (б) ą 9 marked k 10 s, ś free + b 1 l, ł 3 with top cross t 4 struck through c, ć 6 m 7 with top cross u +0 d 3 n, ń 8 struck through w ŧ0 e 8 o, ó 5 with top cross z, ż, ź free ŧ ę 8 with overbar p 7 struck through h (ch = 6 2) 2 f 5 g 7 There are no nulls and no code words. Names and titles are spelled out: Smoleńska , Kró. Mci , W.X.Mci . The index of coincidence over the 1,856 signs is 0.068.
smolensk1633.html#method

A first transcription treated every crossed digit as one sign. On that, a substitution solver scored on a Polish language model gave noise, and so did a reading of the crossed digits as the numbers 10 to 19. With one letter per sign the solver threw up fragments such as wiadomosli , which suggested the signs were the right kind but had been merged. Two cribs then took hold. The clear close has W.X.Mci , and the cipher has the group ŧ0 Δ 7 6 4 four times, which gave w , m , c and i . A twelve-sign word repeated three times fitted nieprzyiaciel if the flagged 6 and the free cross were two letters, r and z . At higher zoom the crosses split by position, and line 1 read straight off as Za gwałtownym i potężnym a barzo ścisłym opasaniem straża murów smoleńskich . Lines 1–7 completed the key, all 24 signs. The page was then transcribed again in the finer classes, and the key was applied mechanically. Words that did not read sent the work back to the image at 3.5–5×. Four were corrected that way: przemysłów , przy uniżonych prozbach , po rożnych and z uniżonemi . A statistical check on the Polish model ( docs/_validate.py ) scores the reading at −2.52 per letter. Random keys score −5.75, and a key fitted to the shuffled ciphertext −4.17 (z 86): a pass. The method counts as a key recovered from adjacent plaintext, because the formula of the clear close was the first crib; everything else came from the cipher.

Za gwałtownym i potężnym a barzo ścisłym opasaniem straża murów smoleńskich przez nieprzyiaciela wysyłać do W.X.M. rzecz barzo trudna, często [?] przez też ostrożności nieprzyiacielskie. I od W.X.Mci długi czas wiadomości nie mamy, co się z nami dzieie w murach. A nieprzyiaciel, iako potężnie [?] nasadziwszy wszytkich swych przemysłów, fortelów, podkopami, z dział biciem, rowów kopaniem iuż pod same mury przyszedszy, usiłuie dobić Smoleńska. […] Zaiste nieszczęśliwiśmy synowie w oyczyźnie […] gdzi obietnice, obowiązki przysiąg senatorskich, żeśmy za kilka niedziel mieli być oswobodzeni przez odsiecz, a teraz iuż to ósmy miesiąc w tey niewoli trwamy, w którey codzień i godzinę [?] wyglądamy zginienia [?] i śmierci pewney [?] od tego okrutnika krzywoprzysiężcy. In English: “Because the enemy has encircled the walls of Smolensk so violently, so powerfully and so very tightly, sending to Your Princely Grace is a very difficult matter, often so because of the enemy’s watchfulness. We have had no news from Your Princely Grace for a long time, nor have you of what is happening to us within the walls. The enemy, having set up all his devices and stratagems, with mines, with the battering of his guns and the digging of trenches, has now come right up to the walls and is trying to finish Smolensk off.” The writers ask the hetman not to let the town, its churches, clergy, children, women, nobility and common people perish through slow relief, since he took its rescue upon himself. They point out that the enemy has split his strength among his camps, earthworks and blockhouses, so a sortie from the walls could join his advance. And they remind him that the senators promised relief within a few weeks, while they are now in the eighth month of the siege.

The second half is probably baczyć (“deign to look to”); the first half is miswritten or misread. A small 1 and two crosses are unclear on the microfilm. Fifteen words rest on one doubtful sign each (82 signs, 4.4%). Most come from the cross positions, which the microfilm blurs: ŧ0 against +0, a plain 4 against a struck 4, and the two crossed 7s. They are listed with their signs in reading.tsv ; each gives sense in its sentence. Whether Sokoliński’s letters printed by Nagielski use the same cipher has not been tested: their originals were not seen. If they do, this key would read them, and the contemporary copy AR dz. II nr 1115 would check this reading. The clear close is only partly transcribed, and the signatures not at all.

Nie dai tak marnie i tak wielkiey [?] liczbie ludzi zginąć przez nierychłe swe dawanie odsieczy, bo żeś W.X.Mć wział na się ratunek mieisca tego. Dufność wielką maiąc w boskiey pomocy, którey skutki iawne [?] W.X.Mć i my utrapieni doznawamy nad tym krzywoprzysiężnym narodem, i to na pomoc, iż on po rożnych swych taborach, szańcach, blokauzach rozerwał swą potęgę, a za nastąpieniem W.X.Mci i z murów smoleńskich według sił naszych posiłek wyniść może. Zaiste nieszczęśliwiśmy synowie w oyczyźnie, i to mieisce sławy pańskiey [?], iż tak marnie do zaginienia bliski pochop ma w oczach woisk iego Król. Mci i W.X.Mci hetmana, oyczyźnie naszey przyległe, a tak długi czas odratowane być nie może, gdzi obietnice, obowiązki przysiąg senatorskich, żeśmy za kilka niedziel mieli być oswobodzeni przez odsiecz, a teraz iuż to ósmy miesiąc w tey niewoli trwamy, w którey codzień i godzinę [?] wyglądamy zginienia [?] i śmierci pewney [?] od tego okrutnika krzywoprzysiężcy. Zatym z uniżonemi prozbami, łzami oblewaiąc się, prze miłosierdzie boże o prętkie odratowanie prosząc. Translation translation_en.md # English translation: the besieged at Smolensk to Krzysztof Radziwiłł, 1 June 1633 A close translation of `reading.md`. Square brackets mark words supplied or doubtful; the one unread group is shown as [...]. Most Illustrious Prince, our most gracious Lord. Because the enemy has encircled the walls of Smolensk so violently, so powerfully and so very tightly, sending to Your Princely Grace is a very difficult matter, and often [?] so because of the enemy's watchfulness. We have also had no news from Your Princely Grace for a long time, nor have you of what is happening to us within the walls. The enemy, having set up [?] all his devices and stratagems, with mines, with the battering of his guns and the digging of trenches, has now come right up to the walls and is trying to finish Smolensk off. Our brother, whom we sent to Your Princely Grace from our midst, will give a full account. We suffer great and very heavy affliction within these walls, through which it is not possible to hold out much longer. To write everything out faithfully is not allowed either, by the very uncertainty of getting letters through; we only lay this before Your Princely Grace, our gracious Lord, with our humble petitions: deign to [...] look to the glory of the Lord, to this place of the fatherland, to the holy churches, the priests, the servants of God, to the innocent little children, the honest maidens, the ladies, to the blood of the nobility, to us afflicted, and to the common people. Do not let so great a number of people perish so miserably through your slowness in sending relief, for Your Princely Grace has taken upon yourself the rescue of this place. Surely the Lord God will require the innocent blood that is shed (God forbid) at Your Princely Grace's hands. The enemy is not so powerful here [?], though he boasts of the strength of his army, that Your Princely Grace could not, with the army of His Royal Majesty, resist him. Having great trust in God's help, whose effects Your Princely Grace and we, the afflicted, plainly experience against this perjured nation, and this in our favour, that he has split his strength among his various camps, earthworks and blockhouses: on Your Princely Grace's advance, a force can also sally out from the walls of Smolensk as far as our strength allows. Truly we are unhappy sons of the fatherland, and this place of the Lord's glory [?] is so miserably near to its ruin, under the eyes of the army of His Royal Majesty and of Your Princely Grace the hetman, adjoining our fatherland; and it cannot be rescued for so long, when the promises and obligations of the senators' oaths were that we should be freed by relief within a few weeks. Now we are already in the eighth month of this captivity, in which every day and hour [?] we await ruin and certain death from this cruel perjurer. Therefore, with humble petitions, bathed in tears, we beg for God's mercy for a speedy rescue. [Clear close:] We commend our service with all urgency [?] to the gracious favour of Your Princely Grace, our gracious Lord. Given from the siege of Smolensk, 1 June 1633. Of Your Princely Grace, our gracious Lord, [the humble servants], followed by the signatures. Key: key.tsv

Three despatches of the French agents at Ferrara in BnF fr. 3096, in a homophonic cipher of geometric signs. George Lasry’s key for the volume was applied; the contribution is the transcription of some 18,000 signs and their decryption, complete for nos. 65 and 66 and partial for no. 63, whose third sheet (f. 123, found by Arya Sanketbhai Patel) reports the Pope near death. A null and a code sign for the duke were added to the key. Alfonso d’Este refuses the crown of Naples and the command of the French army. BnF fr. 3096 is a volume of original letters to François I and Montmorency of 1528–29. Nos. 62 to 67 are the Ferrara file: Sormano’s letters of March 1529 (no. 62, f. 113) and his doppio (no. 67, f. 124) carry a decipherment written between the lines by a contemporary hand; nos. 63 (ff. 115–116), 65 (ff. 119–120) and 66 (ff. 121–122) do not. Tomokiyo’s cryptiana page prints Lasry’s key for the glossed pair and lists the other three as having no contemporary decipherment (no interlinear gloss or nearby deciphered copy). Gallica has the volume at full resolution (btv1b9060015d, views 117–127), 8,660 pixels across a two-page spread, which is about 44 pixels per sign. What this page adds. The key is Lasry’s, and it serves the glossed and the unglossed letters of fr. 3096 alike; applying a volume’s key to its other letters is standard procedure. The same cipher is also used in BnF fr. 3045 f. 28 and fr. 3034 f. 154 (Lasry, personal communication, 21 September 2026); those leaves are not transcribed here. The contribution is the transcription of some 18,000 signs and their decryption, and the null, the code sign and the letter forms that the transcription added to the key. Fr. 3096 f. 121r, the head of no. 66: duplicata in the upper right, the clear opening, and the first cipher runs. The large double circle after si douea and after Don Hercole is the sign for the duke. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3096 f. 121r, via Gallica (btv1b9060015d, view 125). The three letters are one negotiation. No. 65 and no. 66 both open Zobia passata Io Joachin gionsi qua , both subscribe Da Ferrara alli XXIII febraro 1529 , and no. 63 opens Il xxIII del presente per nostre duplicate lettere a vostra Maestà al lungo scrivessimo ciò che havevamo negociato con questo Signor Duca . So 65 and 66 are the duplicate pair sent on the 23rd and 63 is the follow-up. No. 63 breaks off mid-sentence at the foot of f. 116v ( difficilmente crederemo … ), and f. 117 is a different paper in another hand, wholly unciphered. Its last sheet is f. 123, bound after the duplicate: numbered “3” at the foot where ff. 115 and 116 carry “1” and “2”, it continues the broken sentence, ends with the signatures “Sormano, Joachin” and is dated Da Ferr[ara] p[en]ultimo de Febraro M D XXVIIII , the 27th (February had 28 days that year), not the catalogue’s 28th. Its verso carries the address docket. Arya Sanketbhai Patel found this in a separate attempt on the same letters (September 2026), which also showed that no. 64, filed with them, has no cipher at all. Both agents write. The narrative voice moves between Io Joachin and Io Sormano in the same letter, and the passages each man puts in cipher are those about his own audiences. “Joachim de Vaulx” is the Genoese Gian Gioacchino de Passano, seigneur de Vaux, whom the French called Jean Joachim: François I writes to Jean du Bellay of “Monsr de Vaulx, Jean Joaquin”, David Potter’s inventory sends Passano to Ferrara “d’où il écrit le 23 février (BnF, fr. 3096, fo. 119-121)”, and Molini prints a Venice letter in which the writers mention letters “da Ferrara per il Sig. Gaspar Sormano et per me Ioachin” (identification by Patel).

One continuous alphabet of geometric signs written on the line with the clear Italian, no word breaks, cipher and clear alternating mid-sentence. Common letters have three or four homophones: a V υ п 3, e ϰ k Γ 7, i Y ⊙ ρ 4, o Ц 1 ƌ, u/v T α γ H, s Ŧ ⊐; single signs for the rest, Δ c , ▽ q , π n , Q r , x t , 6 p , S g , E h , ϙ l , ꝑ m ; and two doubled letters, ⊡ ll and ≠ cc . That is Lasry’s table, and it is right: the first glossed run on f. 113r, ꜿ f T π Δ V 6 ρ x υ π Γ 1 ⊐ α 4 Δ 7 Q ƌ Δ E ϰ ⊐ , decrypts to de vn capitaneo suicero che s[i] under the gloss d’un capitaneo suizari ch’si , symbol for symbol. The control, f. 113r (no. 62): a cipher run with the decipherer’s gloss above, de vn capitaneo suizari ch’si domanda … . The crossbarred long-s in second place sits under the e of de . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3096 f. 113r, via Gallica (btv1b9060015d, view 117). Four features of the leaves are not in the table, and each causes decryption errors until it is recognised: A null. A tall sign with a large loop and a long descender curling left (ɧ) occurs in all three letters and twice in the second glossed run of no. 62, and carries no letter. H 1 Ǝ x ɧ Q п is vostra ; Δ E ɧ k is che ; Δ ɧ 1 π ſ ʈ Q x ʒ is conforto . The old note “no nulls observed” is struck. A code sign. The large double circle ◎ is a separate sign from the i sign ⊙. It stands for duca everywhere: con questo ◎, fusimo col deto ◎, andai dal deto ◎, circa le cose dil regno ◎ rispondesse . It often falls where the clear hand resumes, which is why it looks like a terminator at first. The fourth e is a crossbarred long-s. It looks like an f and is the commonest letter form on the page; f proper is the double loop ſſ ( offerta , sufficientissime ). Taken as f it corrupts one letter in twelve. ꝓ, the p with a curled tail, is d ( desiderio , dubitai , dal deto ), not an i homophone; and the open C-shaped boxes that the automatic segmentation produced by the hundred are the left half of the r sign Q cut at its tail, not a sign.

No. 66 is not a copy of no. 65. The two were drafted independently from the same notes, and they encipher different stretches . Where no. 65 puts a sentence in cipher, no. 66 very often has it in the clear hand, and the reverse: no. 65, f. 119r (cipher, read here) no. 66, f. 121r (clear on the leaf) maiestà. fata la reuerentia a madama Rainea et al signor don Hercole fatta che hebbimo la reuerentia a Madama Rainea et al s[ignor] Don Hercole suadesimo, confortassimo et instantemente esortasimo et pregasimo suadessemo, confortassemo et instantementi essortassemo et pregassemo nel modo et condicioni in la deta instrittion contenune [sic] nel modo et condition in la ditta instruttion cõtenuti ringratiandola della cosi grande et honorata offerta che gli era piaciuto fargli ringratiandola della cosi grande et honorata offerta che gli era piaciuto fargli The right column was transcribed from the leaf before the left was decrypted, and neither was used to produce the other. It is an independent check on the key and on the glyph transcription, and it settles most of what one copy leaves doubtful. It also means that any future reader with the two leaves side by side can recover most of the pair without a key at all.

Ten page sides at 40–60 signs a line and 35 lines a side is too much to transcribe glyph by glyph from a screen at the resolution Gallica serves, and an earlier pass had stalled at a few lines. The route that worked treats the leaf as a character-recognition problem and leaves the final transcription to the eye: Segmentation. Line bands from the row-ink profile of each side (337 lines, one physical line once split, none missed), then column-ink valleys inside each band, with runs wider than one sign cut at their thinnest points. 18,273 boxes, each cropped to a fixed 100-pixel height about the line’s x-height centre so that ascenders and descenders keep their place. Clustering. Per-line Otsu threshold, blur, 16×22 raster plus width and ink, PCA to 70 dimensions, k-means with 700 centres. Cluster montages ordered by centroid similarity were labelled by eye, letter or “clear hand”, 212 of them automatically from a coarser 340-centre pass, the rest by hand: two sittings of about forty montages. Classification. A k-nearest-neighbour classifier on the labelled glyphs (raster plus gradient-orientation histograms) reassigns every box, including the ones in mixed clusters; five-fold cross-validation on the labelled set gives 90 % letter accuracy, most of the remainder being cipher signs against fragments of the clear cursive rather than sign against sign. A five-glyph majority window then marks each line into cipher and clear runs. Review. For every line a sheet: the magnified strip in two segments, and below it each segmented box with its index and the classifier’s letter. 170 sheets, read in order with the Italian in mind, correcting the letter where the shape or the word required. Every decryption on this page comes from that step; none rests on the classifier alone. Fr. 3096 f. 119r, lines 4–7 of no. 65: ch’ tenir si douea [con questo ◎] / [acioche conclusion si facesse secondo il desiderio di vostra] / [Maiestà. fata la reuerentia a Madama Rainea et al signor don] / [Hercole, fusimo col deto ◎] et presentato le lettere di vra M[aes]tà di credenza . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3096 f. 119r, via Gallica (btv1b9060015d, view 123). The pipeline’s value is in the sheets, not in the decoded string: the classifier’s own line for f. 119r line 4 is acioc*econclvsmns*facesc*so*ondoili… , readable only because one already knows what it should say. Where the segmentation merges two signs or the hand writes one over a descender, the sheet shows it and the eye fixes it; where the signs run for a whole side without a clear word to anchor them, as on no. 63 ff. 115v–116r, the errors compound and the decryption thins to patches.

Fatta la reverentia a Madama Rainea et al signor don Hercole fusimo col detto ◎], et presentato le lettere di vostra Maestà di credenza con quelle conveniente parole che ci parve convenire, esponessimo la nostra credenza et in nome di vostra Maestà [suadesimo, confortassimo et instantemente esortasimo et pregasimo sua Signoria voler accettare quello che lei, come suo buon et affectionato figliolo, ferisse(?) et deliberasse: far l’impresa di Napoli nel modo et condicioni in la detta instruttion contenute]; et qui con molte efficacissime ragion al lungo rimostrassimo [il stabilimento de sua Signoria, suo stato et posterità, l’honor et l’utile che l’une … riportare, et la satisfaction di vostra Maestà, et finalmente il bene, et con gran gloria di sua Signoria, la finale liberatione et quiete de l’Italia]; né gli fu taciuta la grande buon’opera che in beneficio della [sua persona, stato, casa et successione vostra Maestà haveva fatto … et la quasi ferma speranza che lei riteneva in tutto ridure sua Santità … accordi et condicion che … si dicevano et sua Excellentia poteva desiderar], et le qual tutte cose, volendo lei, al lungo gli furon narrate. Sire, benché in quello ragionamento, che fu assai lungo, [circa le cose dil regno ◎ rispondesse di sorte] che dall’hora haressimo possuto scriver quello che hora se dirà, nientedimanco concludendo lui che la cosa [per ◎ … grande ma sua … ricercava tempo per meglio pensarvi, presimo aspettar la sua final risposta, et in sto mezzo fussimo di novo con signor don Hercole et fattogli intender che hora era il tempo di operare in servicio di vostra Maestà et che la sua casa … stato ni toccava tanto … {five lines on Ercole’s own interest, read in patches}] … [avisassemo che io Sormano solo andasse, sì come andai, dal detto ◎ per rimostrargli … dì seguente dimandati fusimo da sua Signoria ◎ … et dipoi molte ragioni che a noi parsero sufficientissime, … solo per rimoverlo da ogni per lei preallegato sospetto, … ma etiam per disponerla a l’accettar di … bon animo quanto per vostra Maestà se gli offeriva]: finalmente, ringratiandola della [così grande et honorata offerta che gli era piaciuto fargli, risolutamente concluse per cosa dil mondo non voler per sé alcunamente accettare il regno et manco far l’impresa a suo nome]; et il parlar suo fu di sorte che [io Sormano mi parvi quasi chiarito di quello che io sempre dubitai, cioè che sua Excellentia, anchora che havesse dato orecchie et risposto] nel modo che io scrissi a vostra Maestà, veramente non havesse [animo d’intendere al capitaneato, del qual già molti giorni haveva ricercato]. Ben disse non solo contentarse ma con ogni instanza pregar vostra Maestà che la volesse [trattar tra lei et lei l’apontamento et accordo, circa el qual disse accettar quanto vostra Maestà facesse, persuadendosi che da quella non serà astretta far se non cosa conveniente et ragionevole]. Sire, per il gran desiderio che noi habbiamo che [questo signor Duca satisfacesse alla espettation de vostra Maestà], et in questo non volendo noi pretermetter alcun’opera et officio né lassar alcuna cosa intentata, non ostante [questa sua detta risposta, da capo fossimo col prefato signor don Hercole, veramente desideroso far servicio a vostra Maestà, … rimostrandogli che tal risposta poco concedeva(?) in alcun suo profitto; del che et lui con noi dolendosi della qualità et risposta del padre, si mostrò poco satisfatto; lo instassimo esser di novo con sua Excellentia, sperando che la non volesse perdere questa che dal tempo et da la liberalità di vostra Maestà se gli offeriva così bella occasion, come qual altra offerirse gli potesse … il suo stato … con suo poco et picolo pericolo … la sua casa et sua successione … Italia, et per satisfar a vostra Maestà] … [per conclusione si confirmò in la sopra scritta fatta risposta, et così mal satisfatto ritirandome … signor don Hercole, che con dir mi come el signor Duca in alcun modo intendere non … per sé, et quanto al capitaneato, non ostante ciò che nel sopra scritto primo ragionamento et poi era stato detto et … risposto, disse che sua Excellentia persisteva in la … forma et modo della risposta a questi dì data a me Sormano … così poco … risoluto et poco chiaro come la … fu data, toccando … accordo … componere le cose sue col …]. Sire, dalli soprascritti ragionamenti havuti con questo signor Duca pare di poter concluder che [non si possa far … fondamento che in effetto el … voler intrar o accettar el capitaneato, sul quale … provisione, circonstance et sue dependentie dal canto di sua Excellentia se … le difficultà, et a nostro giudicio … la cosa insieme con le sue provision … dependentie così difficile che paia … di difficultà, et non la volontà sia … quel che non lo facino accettar … questa nostra per aventura vana opinion] a vostra Maestà non c’è parso tacere. Io Joachin aspettarò qua il signor Marechial Triulzo, et siamo d’openione che sua Signoria, [dal prefato signor Duca molto stimata, a beneficio di questa cosa con sua Excellentia s’adoperi], il che per ben di questo negocio et servicio di vostra Maestà siamo certi farà ben volentieri. Da Ferrara alli XXIII febraro MDXXVIIII. English Last Thursday I, Jean Joachim, arrived here and went straight to the lodging of the ambassador messer Gaspare Sormano, where I am staying; I gave him your Majesty’s intention and commission and showed him your instruction and mandate, and having talked it over at length we settled how to proceed [with this Duke so that a conclusion might be reached as your Majesty wishes. Having paid our respects to Madame Renée and to Don Ercole we went to the Duke], presented your Majesty’s letters of credence with such fitting words as seemed right, set out our credence and in your Majesty’s name [urged, encouraged and most insistently exhorted and begged his Lordship to accept what he, as your good and affectionate son, should resolve upon: to make the enterprise of Naples in the manner and on the conditions contained in the instruction]. We showed him at length [the securing of his Lordship, his state and his posterity, the honour and the profit that would follow, your Majesty’s satisfaction, and finally, with great glory to his Lordship, the final liberation and quiet of Italy]; nor was he left ignorant of the great good that your Majesty had done [for his person, state, house and succession … and the nearly firm hope you held of bringing his Holiness wholly round … to terms and conditions that … his Excellency could desire]; all of which, since he wished it, was told him at length. Sire, although in that conversation, which was very long, [on the matters of the kingdom the Duke answered in such a way] that we could have written then what will now be said, still, he concluding that so [great] a matter needed time for reflection, [we resolved to await his final answer, and meanwhile went again to Don Ercole and let him know that now was the time to act in your Majesty’s service, and that his house … and his state were so much concerned …]. [We agreed that I, Sormano, should go alone, as I did, to the Duke, to show him … The next day we were summoned by his Lordship the Duke … and after many reasons which seemed to us more than sufficient, … not only to remove every suspicion he alleged, … but also to dispose him to accept with good will what your Majesty offered him]: in the end, thanking you for [so great and honourable an offer, he resolutely concluded that for nothing in the world would he in any way accept the kingdom for himself, nor make the enterprise in his own name]; and his manner of speaking was such that [I, Sormano, thought myself almost certain of what I had always doubted, namely that his Excellency, though he had lent an ear and answered] as I wrote to your Majesty, never truly [meant to take up the captaincy, which he had been asked for many days before]. He did say that he would not only be content but would beg your Majesty with every insistence [to treat between yourself and him the appointment and accord, and said he would accept whatever your Majesty did, being persuaded that you would bind him to nothing but what is fitting and reasonable]. Sire, out of our great wish that [this Duke should satisfy your Majesty’s expectation], leaving nothing untried, notwithstanding [this answer we went back to Don Ercole, who truly wishes to serve your Majesty …, showing him how little such an answer served his own profit; and he, grieving with us over the nature of his father’s answer, showed himself ill satisfied; we pressed him to go again to his Excellency, hoping he would not let slip so fair an occasion as your Majesty’s liberality and the times offered him … his state … at small and little risk … his house and his succession … Italy, and to satisfy your Majesty]. [In conclusion the Duke confirmed his earlier answer, and I, Sormano, withdrew ill satisfied … Don Ercole telling me that the Duke would in no way take it on for himself, and that as to the captaincy, whatever had been said and answered before, his Excellency held to the form of the reply given me some days ago, … as little resolved and as little clear as when it was given, touching on … an accord … to settle his affairs with the Pope …]. Sire, from all these conversations with the Duke it seems we may conclude that [no reliance can be placed on his in fact meaning to enter or accept the captaincy; on which, as to the provisions, circumstances and dependencies, on his Excellency’s side the difficulties … and in our judgement … the thing, with all its provisions and dependencies, is so difficult that it seems … it is difficulty and not want of will … that keeps him from accepting; this our perhaps vain opinion] we thought it right not to hide from your Majesty. I, Joachim, shall wait here for the marshal Trivulzio, and we are of opinion that his Lordship, [much esteemed by the Duke, will exert himself with his Excellency for this business], which for the good of the affair and your Majesty’s service we are sure he will do very willingly. From Ferrara, 23 February 1529. Madama Rainea is Renée de France, Louis XII’s daughter, married to Ercole d’Este in 1528; questo signor Duca is Alfonso I d’Este; il Marechial Triulzo is Teodoro Trivulzio, marshal of France and governor of Genoa. The capitaneato is the command of the French army in the kingdom of Naples after Lautrec’s death before the city in August 1528, when the King was looking for an Italian prince to carry the war; the crown of Naples was the bait. Alfonso’s refusal here, dressed in the want of provisions, is the first sign of the turn that ended with his abandonment of the French alliance and his accommodation with the Emperor at the Peace of Cambrai (August 1529) and the settlement of 1530.

No. 66 tells the same story in the same order, with the clear and ciphered stretches swapped as described above, and a fuller close: Non mancaremo continuamente sollicitar sua Excellentia, et se da quella altro potremo haver se dira . The reading audit of 22 October 2026 found its own cipher stretches to be letter strings that mostly made no words, and set it to decoded, not read. On 23 October every cipher stretch of ff. 121r–122r was re-read sign by sign on the Gallica master (the old f. 121r strings were misreadings, and f. 121v lines 21–43 and f. 122r had never been transcribed), using no. 65 only as a check. Three values hold across the letter: the crossbarred long-s is a null (about twenty places), a looped b-shaped sign is rr ( ridure , Ferara , l’errore ) and a looped Ʒ is z ; a code sign read Papa (four contexts) and another [?Imperatore] (one) rest on context and are flagged. No. 66 now reads ( no66_reading.md , English no66_en.md ); nothing in it changes the account. No. 63 is the sequel and the hardest of the three: four sides, three of them almost solid cipher, no sibling. The decrypted part is enough for the sense. The duke had given “poco chiara [?et] risoluta risposta” on the captaincy and repeats it; he says he cannot see that the King and his confederates are making the provisions the enterprise needs, … esercito in campagna … , money for Swiss, Spaniards and Genoese, and that all should be furnished before he commits, et tanto più hora, che già siamo — così disse — nel buon tempo . Two things he asks the King to remember, one about the Naples enterprise itself and one about the command. Dal canto suo disse non dover mancare ; the agents say they have omitted nothing in their power, judge from the duke’s nature that the matter debba esser non poco difficile , and put their hope in Trivulzio: Sire, con tutto che per le ragion dette siamo in … poca speranza che questo signor duca … intendere … capitaneato, pur in questa causa non volendo noi pretermetter alcuna natura d’opera et d’ufficio, se’l signor Marechial Triulzo andando a Vinetia passarà per qua … pensiamo operar che sua Signoria …; et in sto mezzo per tri o quatro giorni anchora Io Joachin qui l’espettarò . Its second sheet stops at the foot of f. 116v in the middle of a clause, which continues on f. 123r (next section). The decipherment of ff. 115–116, with the undecrypted runs marked, is targets/sormano/n63_reading.md . Read only in patches, ff. 115–116 are decoded, not read . On 23 October 2026 f. 115r lines 1–27 were re-read sign by sign with the values found in no. 66 ( no63_reading.md , partial); the rest of the two leaves has not yet been reached, and the image is legible enough to do it.

Before the key was found, Arya Sanketbhai Patel worked on the same three letters from the Gallica images (September 2026; his notes and scripts are in targets/sormano/arya/ ). From the margin decipherment of no. 67 and the gloss on no. 62 he fixed 22 values, thirteen of them twice over, and checked them on a sentence that no. 66 has in clear and no. 65 in cipher. Against Lasry’s table, 20 of the 22 are right; the two wrong ones (the figure 4 is i , not e ; the figure 3 is a , not o ) were what had blocked him. His eight attempts to finish the key without it, from mask overlap and template matching to a language-model decoder, all failed on homophone forms that the microfilm does not separate; the language-model output was fluent Italian and wholly invented, a warning for any decipherment of these leaves offered without its sign-level evidence. Fr. 3096 f. 124r, no. 67: Sormano’s copy of his letter to the Duke of Urbino, four lines of cipher tied to a decipherment down the left margin, un cappitaneo suizzeri nominato calzolite ch al p[rese]nto si retrovava ne l’aquila… , about 161 letters against 161 signs. Lasry’s exemplar table for Sormano’s cipher: four forms each for a , e , i and u/v , three for o , two for s , and signs for cc and ll . Image: Table by George Lasry (2023), built from BnF fr. 3096 f. 113, via S. Tomokiyo, Cryptiana. He also found two further leads. On f. 116v the words de Venetiani are written above a two-sign group, a third contemporary gloss that shows the cipher had a nomenclator beyond the duke’s sign. And Molini’s Documenti di storia italiana prints, with its interlinear decipherment in italics, Sormano’s letter from Ferrara of 13 April 1529 in the same cipher (BnF fr. 2974 f. 94, on microfiche only); Molini does not print nos. 63, 65 or 66.

In no. 65 about a dozen words are marked (?) or left in braces: the five lines on Ercole’s interest at the foot of f. 119r, three lines at the foot of f. 119v, and the run on f. 120r where the duke’s answer is repeated. All are places where the segmentation merged or split signs in a dense run; the glyph strings are in the transcription. No. 66’s re-reading shows these signs are legible (no. 65’s {B} is the rr sign), so they can be re-read the same way. No. 63 ff. 115–116: decoded, not read; roughly half the cipher lines are decrypted only in patches. Lines 1–27 of f. 115r were re-read sign by sign on 23 October 2026; the rest still needs it. The Gallica master is legible at 1–1.8×, and no. 66’s values read it. The b sign (τ) was not securely identified on any leaf; the few b ’s in the text fall in words restored from context ( buon , bene , bella ). The dates: 23 February 1529 is on the leaves for 65 and 66; no. 63 is dated on its third sheet, f. 123r, penultimo February, the 27th. f. 123r: three signs before ricaduto give no word; rima{s}a rests on a B-shaped sign not in the table; sera fato could be sera dato if the tall looped sign is d ; and the crossbarred long-s is a null there, as in no. 66 (about twenty places), against the e fixed on f. 113r, which needs a recheck.

Da Ferrara alli XXIII febraro MDXXVIIII. ### Summary (English) 1. De Vaulx arrived on Thursday, joined the resident Sormano, and they agreed how to approach Duke Alfonso so that a conclusion could be reached as the King wished. 2. After paying their respects to Renée de France and Ercole d'Este they delivered the King's letters of credence and urged the duke to accept, "as the King's good and affectionate son", the enterprise of Naples on the terms of their instruction. 3. They set out the arguments: the security of his house and state, honour and profit, the King's satisfaction, the liberation and quiet of Italy, and all the King had done for his person, state, house and succession, including the hope of reconciling him with the Pope. 4. The duke answered at length but asked for time on so great a matter; the agents pressed Ercole meanwhile. 5. Sormano then saw the duke alone; after many reasons the duke declared that for nothing in the world would he accept the kingdom for himself or make the enterprise in his own name. 6. Sormano says this confirmed his long-standing doubt that the duke ever meant to accept the captaincy he had been asked for. 7. The duke offered only to accept whatever settlement the King negotiated on his behalf with the Pope, trusting the King to ask nothing unreasonable. 8. The agents went back to Ercole, who was unhappy with his father's answer and agreed to press him again — without result: the duke persisted in his earlier, unclear and unresolved reply. 9. The agents conclude that no reliance can be placed on the duke's accepting the captaincy; his difficulties are, in their view, pretexts. 10. De Vaulx will await marshal Trivulzio, whom the duke esteems, and hope he can move him. Ferrara, 23 February 1529. ## Cross-check against no. 66 no. 66 f. 121r L6–7 has in the clear hand *"fatta che hebbimo la reuerentia a Madama Rainea et al s[ignor] Don Hercole"*, and L10 *"suadessemo confortassemo et instantementi essortassemo et pregassemo"*. These are the same two sentences read above out of no. 65's cipher at L5 and L9–10. The decipherment and the duplicate confirm each other. ## Persons *Madama Rainea* — Renée de France, duchess of Ferrara. *don Hercole* — Ercole d'Este. *Gaspar Sormano* — the resident ambassador. *Jo Gian Joachino* — Joachim de Vaulx, newly arrived with the king's instruction and mandate. The English follows the gaps rather than filling them. --> # No. 65, Sormano and de Vaulx to François I, Ferrara, 23 February 1529 (BnF fr. 3096 ff. 119-120): English translation ### f. 119r Last Thursday I, Gian Joachino, arrived here and went straight to the lodging of the ambassador messer Gaspar Sormano, where I am; and having communicated to him Your Majesty's intention and commission, and shown him its instruction and mandate, and having discussed at length between us and settled the way to proceed *with this* ◎, *so that a conclusion might be reached according to Your Majesty's desire: having paid our respects to Madame Renée and to the lord Don Ercole, we were with the said* ◎, and having presented Your Majesty's letters of credence with such fitting words as seemed fitting to us, we set out our credence, and in Your Majesty's name *we persuaded, encouraged, and earnestly exhorted and begged His Lordship to be willing to accept what he, as his good and affectionate son, should ferisse(?) and resolve: to make the enterprise of Naples in the manner and on the conditions contained in the said instruction*; and here, with many most effective reasons, we showed at length *the establishment of His Lordship, his state and posterity, the honour and the profit that the one … bring back, and Your Majesty's satisfaction, and finally the good, and, with great glory to His Lordship, the final liberation and quiet of Italy*; nor was he left untold of the great good work that, for the benefit of *his person, state, house and succession, Your Majesty had done with … and the almost firm hope that she held of bringing His Holiness wholly round … agreements and conditions that … were spoken of and His Excellency could desire* — and all of which things, as he wished, were related to him at length. Sire, although in that discussion, which was quite long, *concerning the affairs of the kingdom* ◎ *answered in such a way* that from then on we could have written what will now be said, nevertheless, as he concluded that the matter *for* ◎ *… great but his … required time to think it over better, we decided to await his final answer; and meanwhile we were again with the lord Don Ercole and let him understand that now was the time to work in Your Majesty's service, and that his house … and his … state concerned him so much …* 《f. 119r L32-36: the run on Ercole's own interest — his house, his person, what he might hope for — is only partly legible》 ### f. 119v *… we advised that I, Sormano, should go alone, as I went, to the said* ◎ *to show him how to a … servant the … that His Excellency do … when … what is said. … the following day we were asked by His Lordship* ◎ *… and after many reasons that seemed to us most sufficient, … only to remove him from every suspicion alleged earlier by him, … as … naturally … said and … but also to dispose him to accept with … good heart what was offered him by Your Majesty*: finally, thanking her for *so great and honourable an offer as it had pleased her to make him, he concluded resolutely that for nothing in the world would he accept the kingdom for himself in any way, still less make the enterprise in his own name*; and his speech was such that *I, Sormano, seemed to myself almost cleared up about what I always suspected, namely that His Excellency, although he had given ear and answered* in the way I wrote to Your Majesty, truly had no *mind to undertake the captaincy, of which many days ago he had been sounded.* He did say that he not only was content but begged Your Majesty with all insistence to be willing *to negotiate, between her and him(?), the settlement and agreement, about which he said he would accept whatever Your Majesty did, persuading himself that he would not be constrained by her to do anything but what is fitting and reasonable*. Sire, because of the great desire we have that *this lord Duke should satisfy Your Majesty's expectation*, and not wishing to omit any work or office in this, nor leave anything untried, notwithstanding *this said answer of his, we were again with the aforesaid lord Don Ercole, truly desirous to do Your Majesty service, and … not … content …, showing him that such an answer conceded(?) little to any profit of his; at which he too, lamenting with us the quality of his father's answer, showed himself little satisfied; we urged him to be with His Excellency again, hoping that he would not want to lose this so fine occasion that time and Your Majesty's liberality offered him, as any other could be offered him … his state … with little and small danger to him … his house and his succession … Italy, and to satisfy Your Majesty*; besides this, I advised that *I, Sormano, another time …* 《…》 ◎ 《…》 ### f. 120r *… in conclusion he confirmed himself in the answer written above; and so, ill satisfied, withdrawing myself … to a person … the lord Don Ercole, who, telling me how the lord Duke in no way [would] undertake … for himself; and as for the captaincy, notwithstanding what had been said and … answered in the first discussion written above and afterwards, he said that His Excellency persisted in the … form and manner of the answer given to me, Sormano, in these days …, if said I wrote it in that very manner, and so little … resolved and little clear as the … was given, touching … they will make … agreement … to compose his affairs with the …, telling me as much as above.* Sire, from the above-written discussions held with this lord Duke it seems possible to conclude that *no … foundation can be made that in effect the … wish to enter or accept the captaincy, on which … provision, circumstances and their dependencies on His Excellency's side … the difficulties; and in our judgement, for … the thing together with its provisions … dependencies so difficult that it seems … of difficulty, and not the will be … what makes him not accept … this perhaps vain opinion of ours* it did not seem to us right to keep silent from Your Majesty. I, Joachin, will await the lord Marshal Trivulzio here, and we are of the opinion that His Lordship, *much esteemed by the aforesaid lord Duke, will exert himself with His Excellency for the benefit of this matter*, which, for the good of this business and Your Majesty's service, we are certain he will very willingly do. From Ferrara, the 23rd of February 1529. Spelling is the leaf's. ## Reading ### f. 121r Zobia passata Jo Joachin gionsi qua, et drito me ne veni al logiamento del Ambassator messer Gaspar Sorman, nel quale mi truovo, et a lui comunicata l'intention et comission di vostra Maestà, et mostratagli l'instruttion et mandato di quella, et tra nui al lungo divisato et preso ordine dil modo che tenir si dovea *con* [Duca] *per che conclusion si facese secondo il desiderio di vostra maiesta*. Fatta che hebbimo la reverentia a Madama Rainea et al signor Don Hercole *fosimo col prefato* [Duca], et presentate le credential lettere di vostra Maestà, con quelle conveniente parole che ci parve convenire esponessimo la nostra credenza, et *in nome di vostra maiesta* suadessemo, confortassemo et instantemente essortassemo et pregassemo *sua excelentia voler accettar quello che lei come suo buon et afectionato parente gli oferiva, et deliberarsi d'accettar quello: far l'impresa di Napoli* nel modo et condition in la ditta instruttion contenuti. Et qui con molte efficacissime ragion al lungo rimostrassimo *il stabilimento di sua excelenza, suo stato et [?posterita], l'honor et l'utile che ne riportarebe*, la satisfattion di vostra Maestà, et finalmente *il ben et con gran gloria soa la final liberation et quiete d'Italia*. Ne gli fu taciuta la grande opera che in beneficio della sua persona, stato, casa et successione vostra Maestà havea fatto *col* [Papa] *et la quasi ferma speranza che lei teneva in tuto ridure sua santita a quello accordo et condicion* che si dicevano et sua Excellentia posseva desiderar, et le qual tutte, cosi volendo lei, al lungo gli furon narrate. Sire, benche in quello ragionamento, che fu assai lungo, *circa la cosa del regno* sua Excellentia rispondesse di sorte che dall'hora haresimo possuto scriver quello che hora si dira, nientedimanco concludendo lei che la cosa per la grandezza sua ricercava tempo per meglio pensarvi, presimo aspettar la sua final risposta. Et in sto mezzo col signor Don Hercole di nuovo fossimo, et fattogli intender che *hora era il tempo per operarse in servicio di vostra maiesta*, et in che cosa, in cosa *d'honor, d'utile, stabilimento et exaltation dil nome, casa et stato di Ferara*, che da mo *suo si poseva dire*, et certo che sua Signoria di buon cuore ci promisse, et crediamo che ci habbi prestato ogni sua opera et ufficio. Non contenti di questa opera avisassimo che *io Sormano solo andasi, si come andai, dal deto signor duca per rimostrargli come amorevole servitore l'errore che sua excelentia farebe quando la non accetase ciò che se dice*. Di seguente dimandati fussimo da sua Excellentia, et di poi molte ragione che a noi parsero sufficientissime, no solo per rimoverlo da ogni per lei prealegato *sospeto si del* [Papa] *come de* [?Imperatore] naturalmente, come diceva et dice, *suoi nimici*, ma etiam ### f. 121v *per disponerla a l'accettar di buon animo quanto per* vostra Maestà *se gli* [o]*feriva*, finalmente ringratiandola della cosi grande et honorata offerta che gli era piaciuto fargli, risolutamente concluse *per cosa del mondo non voler per se alcunamente accettare il regno et manco far l'impresa a suo nome*. Et il parlar suo fu di sorte che Jo Sormano mi parve quasi *chiaro di quello che sempre dubitai*, cioe che sua Excellentia, anchora che *l'havesse dato orechie et risposo nel modo che io scrisi a* vostra Maestà, veramente *non havesse animo d'intender al capitaneato*, del qual gia molti giorni Jo l'haveva ricercato. Ben disse no solo contentarsi, ma con ogni instanza pregar vostra Maestà che la volesse *tratar tra* [Papa] *et lei l'apontamento et accordo*, circa il quale disse dover *accetar quanto* vostra Maestà *facese*, persuadendosi che da quella no sara astretta far se no cosa conveniente et ragionevole. Sire, per il gran desiderio che noi habbiamo che [Duca] *satisfacese a lla espectation di* vostra Maestà, et in questo no volendo noi pretermetter alcuna opera et ufficio ne la[ssar] alcuna cosa intentata, no ostante la su detta havuta risposta, da capo fossimo dal prefato signor Don Hercole, veramente desideroso far servicio a vostra Maestà, et su la nostra *non buona contenteza* rimostrandogli che *tal risposta poco cedeva in alcun suo profito*, del che et *lui con noi dolendosi della qualita et risposta dil patre si mostro poco satisfato*, lo instassimo esser di nuovo con sua Excellentia, operando che *la non volese perdere questa che dal tempo et dalla liberalita di vostra* Maestà *se gli* [o]*feriva cosi bella occasion, come qual altra oferir mai se gli potese, si per stabilir le cose sue, esaltar con suo poco et picolo pericolo et minor spesa sua casa et successione*, come per *liberar Italia et per satisfar a* vostra Maestà. Oltra di questo avisassemo che *io Sormano* un altra volta mi *trovase, come mi trovai, solo col deto* [Duca] per avertirlo di nuovo di cio che a beneficio di questo negocio convenir mi pareva. Hor havendo seco al lungo dibatuto il caso, sua Excellentia per conclusion si confirmo *nella sopra scrita fata risposta, et cosi mal satisfato* ritornandomi da lui, poco apresso a noi arriva il signor Don Hercole, che ci confirmo come *il signor duca in alcun modo intender non voleva al regno per se; [?quanto] al capitaneato*, non ostante cio che nel soprascritto primo ragionamento et poi era stato ditto et risposto, disse che sua Excellentia persisteva *in la forma et modo della risposta a questi di data a me Sormano, la qual*, come s'e detto, Jo scrissi in quello proprio modo, *et cosi poco risoluto et poco chiaro* come la mi fu data. Toccante mo il far *accordo et componere le cose soe con* [Papa], confirmo quanto di sopra s'e detto. ### f. 122r Sire, dalli soprascritti ragionamenti havuti con questo signor Duca par da posser concluder che *non si sia da far gran fondamento che in effeto el deba voler intrar o accetar il capitaneato, sul quale provision, circonstance et sue dependentie dal canto di sua excelentia se n'aducano tute le dificulta*, et a nostro giudicio *per prendere la cosa insieme co le sue provisione et dependentie cosi dificile che paia che le dificulta, et non la volunta, sian quelle che nol facin accetare; et questa nostra per aventura vana opinione a vostra maiesta non c'e parso tacer*. Non mancaremo continuamente sollicitar sua Excellentia, et se da quella altro potremo haver se dira. Jo Joachin qua aspettaro il signor Marechial Triulzo, et siamo d'openione che sua Signoria, dal prefato signor Duca molto stimata, a beneficio di questa causa s'adopri; il che, per ben di questo negocio et servicio di vostra Maestà, siamo certi fara ben volentiera. Da Ferrara alli 23 Febraro 1529. ## Notes - [Duca] is the nomenclator ◎ (KEY.md); [Papa] the code sign ⊬7, [?Imperatore] a curled saltire, both identified from context only (flagged in `no66_reread_log.md`). - *Ferara*, *ridure* and *l'errore* carry the new Б = rr sign; *soa*/*soe* are the leaf's forms of *sua*/*sue*. - *se gli feriva* stands twice in the figures; the *o* of *oferiva* is supplied. Spelling is the leaf's. ## Reading ### f. 121r Zobia passata Jo Joachin gionsi qua, et drito me ne veni al logiamento del Ambassator messer Gaspar Sorman, nel quale mi truovo, et a lui comunicata l'intention et comission di vostra Maestà, et mostratagli l'instruttion et mandato di quella, et tra nui al lungo divisato et preso ordine dil modo che tenir si dovea *con* [Duca] *per che conclusion si facese secondo il desiderio di vostra maiesta*. Fatta che hebbimo la reverentia a Madama Rainea et al signor Don Hercole *fosimo col prefato* [Duca], et presentate le credential lettere di vostra Maestà, con quelle conveniente parole che ci parve convenire esponessimo la nostra credenza, et *in nome di vostra maiesta* suadessemo, confortassemo et instantemente essortassemo et pregassemo *sua excelentia voler accettar quello che lei come suo buon et afectionato parente gli oferiva, et deliberarsi d'accettar quello: far l'impresa di Napoli* nel modo et condition in la ditta instruttion contenuti. Et qui con molte efficacissime ragion al lungo rimostrassimo *il stabilimento di sua excelenza, suo stato et [?posterita], l'honor et l'utile che ne riportarebe*, la satisfattion di vostra Maestà, et finalmente *il ben et con gran gloria soa la final liberation et quiete d'Italia*. Ne gli fu taciuta la grande opera che in beneficio della sua persona, stato, casa et successione vostra Maestà havea fatto *col* [Papa] *et la quasi ferma speranza che lei teneva in tuto ridure sua santita a quello accordo et condicion* che si dicevano et sua Excellentia posseva desiderar, et le qual tutte, cosi volendo lei, al lungo gli furon narrate. Sire, benche in quello ragionamento, che fu assai lungo, *circa la cosa del regno* sua Excellentia rispondesse di sorte che dall'hora haresimo possuto scriver quello che hora si dira, nientedimanco concludendo lei che la cosa per la grandezza sua ricercava tempo per meglio pensarvi, presimo aspettar la sua final risposta. Et in sto mezzo col signor Don Hercole di nuovo fossimo, et fattogli intender che *hora era il tempo per operarse in servicio di vostra maiesta*, et in che cosa, in cosa *d'honor, d'utile, stabilimento et exaltation dil nome, casa et stato di Ferara*, che da mo *suo si poseva dire*, et certo che sua Signoria di buon cuore ci promisse, et crediamo che ci habbi prestato ogni sua opera et ufficio. Non contenti di questa opera avisassimo che *io Sormano solo andasi, si come andai, dal deto signor duca per rimostrargli come amorevole servitore l'errore che sua excelentia farebe quando la non accetase ciò che se dice*. Di seguente dimandati fussimo da sua Excellentia, et di poi molte ragione che a noi parsero sufficientissime, no solo per rimoverlo da ogni per lei prealegato *sospeto si del* [Papa] *come de* [?Imperatore] naturalmente, come diceva et dice, *suoi nimici*, ma etiam ### f. 121v *per disponerla a l'accettar di buon animo quanto per* vostra Maestà *se gli* [o]*feriva*, finalmente ringratiandola della cosi grande et honorata offerta che gli era piaciuto fargli, risolutamente concluse *per cosa del mondo non voler per se alcunamente accettare il regno et manco far l'impresa a suo nome*. Et il parlar suo fu di sorte che Jo Sormano mi parve quasi *chiaro di quello che sempre dubitai*, cioe che sua Excellentia, anchora che *l'havesse dato orechie et risposo nel modo che io scrisi a* vostra Maestà, veramente *non havesse animo d'intender al capitaneato*, del qual gia molti giorni Jo l'haveva ricercato. Ben disse no solo contentarsi, ma con ogni instanza pregar vostra Maestà che la volesse *tratar tra* [Papa] *et lei l'apontamento et accordo*, circa il quale disse dover *accetar quanto* vostra Maestà *facese*, persuadendosi che da quella no sara astretta far se no cosa conveniente et ragionevole. Sire, per il gran desiderio che noi habbiamo che [Duca] *satisfacese a lla espectation di* vostra Maestà, et in questo no volendo noi pretermetter alcuna opera et ufficio ne la[ssar] alcuna cosa intentata, no ostante la su detta havuta risposta, da capo fossimo dal prefato signor Don Hercole, veramente desideroso far servicio a vostra Maestà, et su la nostra *non buona contenteza* rimostrandogli che *tal risposta poco cedeva in alcun suo profito*, del che et *lui con noi dolendosi della qualita et risposta dil patre si mostro poco satisfato*, lo instassimo esser di nuovo con sua Excellentia, operando che *la non volese perdere questa che dal tempo et dalla liberalita di vostra* Maestà *se gli* [o]*feriva cosi bella occasion, come qual altra oferir mai se gli potese, si per stabilir le cose sue, esaltar con suo poco et picolo pericolo et minor spesa sua casa et successione*, come per *liberar Italia et per satisfar a* vostra Maestà. Oltra di questo avisassemo che *io Sormano* un altra volta mi *trovase, come mi trovai, solo col deto* [Duca] per avertirlo di nuovo di cio che a beneficio di questo negocio convenir mi pareva. Hor havendo seco al lungo dibatuto il caso, sua Excellentia per conclusion si confirmo *nella sopra scrita fata risposta, et cosi mal satisfato* ritornandomi da lui, poco apresso a noi arriva il signor Don Hercole, che ci confirmo come *il signor duca in alcun modo intender non voleva al regno per se; [?quanto] al capitaneato*, non ostante cio che nel soprascritto primo ragionamento et poi era stato ditto et risposto, disse che sua Excellentia persisteva *in la forma et modo della risposta a questi di data a me Sormano, la qual*, come s'e detto, Jo scrissi in quello proprio modo, *et cosi poco risoluto et poco chiaro* come la mi fu data. Toccante mo il far *accordo et componere le cose soe con* [Papa], confirmo quanto di sopra s'e detto. ### f. 122r Sire, dalli soprascritti ragionamenti havuti con questo signor Duca par da posser concluder che *non si sia da far gran fondamento che in effeto el deba voler intrar o accetar il capitaneato, sul quale provision, circonstance et sue dependentie dal canto di sua excelentia se n'aducano tute le dificulta*, et a nostro giudicio *per prendere la cosa insieme co le sue provisione et dependentie cosi dificile che paia che le dificulta, et non la volunta, sian quelle che nol facin accetare; et questa nostra per aventura vana opinione a vostra maiesta non c'e parso tacer*. Non mancaremo continuamente sollicitar sua Excellentia, et se da quella altro potremo haver se dira. Jo Joachin qua aspettaro il signor Marechial Triulzo, et siamo d'openione che sua Signoria, dal prefato signor Duca molto stimata, a beneficio di questa causa s'adopri; il che, per ben di questo negocio et servicio di vostra Maestà, siamo certi fara ben volentiera. Da Ferrara alli 23 Febraro 1529. ## Notes - [Duca] is the nomenclator ◎ (KEY.md); [Papa] the code sign ⊬7, [?Imperatore] a curled saltire, both identified from context only (flagged in `no66_reread_log.md`). - *Ferara*, *ridure* and *l'errore* carry the new Б = rr sign; *soa*/*soe* are the leaf's forms of *sua*/*sue*. - *se gli feriva* stands twice in the figures; the *o* of *oferiva* is supplied.
