Modern spelling here only. ### f. 121r Last Thursday I, Joachim, arrived here and went straight to the lodging of the ambassador Messer Gaspar Sormano, where I am now staying. I told him Your Majesty's intention and commission and showed him the instruction and mandate, and between us we discussed at length and settled how to proceed *with the [Duke] so that a conclusion might be reached as Your Majesty desires*. After paying our respects to Madame Renée and Lord Don Ercole, *we went to the aforesaid [Duke]*. We presented Your Majesty's letters of credence with fitting words and set out our credence, and *in Your Majesty's name* we persuaded, encouraged, earnestly exhorted and begged *His Excellency to accept what Your Majesty, as his good and affectionate kinsman, was offering him, and to resolve to accept it: to undertake the enterprise of Naples* on the terms and conditions in the instruction. With many very strong arguments we showed him at length *the security of His Excellency, his state and [?posterity], and the honour and profit he would draw from it*, Your Majesty's satisfaction, and finally *the good, with great glory to him, of the final liberation and peace of Italy*. Nor did we pass over the great work Your Majesty had done for his person, state, house and succession *with the [Pope], and the almost firm hope he held of bringing His Holiness entirely to the agreement and conditions* that were being discussed and that His Excellency could wish for. All of this, at his wish, was told him at length. Sire, although in that discussion, which was very long, His Excellency answered *on the matter of the kingdom* in such a way that we could have written then what will now be said, nonetheless, since he concluded that so great a matter needed time for more thought, we decided to wait for his final answer. Meanwhile we went again to Lord Don Ercole and made him understand that *now was the time to exert himself in Your Majesty's service*, and in what: in matters *of honour, profit, security and exaltation of the name, house and state of Ferrara*, which from now on *could be called his*. He promised us wholeheartedly, and we believe he has given all his effort. Not content with this, we advised that *I, Sormano, should go alone, as I did, to the said Lord Duke, to show him as a loving servant the error His Excellency would make if he did not accept what is proposed*. The next day we were sent for by His Excellency, and after many reasons that seemed to us more than sufficient, not only to free him of the *suspicion, as he alleged, of the [Pope] and of the [?Emperor]*, naturally, as he said and still says, *his enemies*, but also ### f. 121v *to dispose him to accept with good heart what Your Majesty* was offering him, he finally thanked Your Majesty for the great and honourable offer it had pleased you to make, and resolutely concluded *that for nothing in the world would he accept the kingdom for himself, still less undertake the enterprise in his own name*. His speech was such that I, Sormano, felt almost *certain of what I had always suspected*: that His Excellency, although *he had given ear and answered in the way I wrote to* Your Majesty, truly *had no mind to take up the captaincy*, which I had been asking of him for many days. He did say that he would not only be content but begged Your Majesty with all insistence *to negotiate between the [Pope] and himself the settlement and agreement*, and as to that he said he would *accept whatever* Your Majesty *did*, trusting that you would not compel him to anything but what was fitting and reasonable. Sire, from our great wish that the [Duke] *should meet Your Majesty's expectation*, and wanting to leave no effort or office undone and nothing untried, despite that answer we went again to the aforesaid Lord Don Ercole, who truly wishes to serve Your Majesty, and on *our great discontent* we showed him that *such an answer brought him little profit*. At this *he, lamenting with us the nature of his father's answer, showed himself little satisfied*, and we urged him to go again to His Excellency and work so that *he would not lose this opportunity, which time and Your Majesty's liberality were offering him, as fine as any other that could ever be offered him, both to secure his affairs and to exalt, with little and small danger and less expense, his house and succession*, and *to free Italy and to satisfy* Your Majesty. Besides this we advised that *I, Sormano*, should once again *find myself, as I did, alone with the said [Duke]* to warn him again of what seemed to me fitting for this business. Having debated the case with him at length, His Excellency in conclusion confirmed himself *in the answer written above, and so, ill satisfied*, I returned. Shortly after, Lord Don Ercole came to us and confirmed that *the Lord Duke would in no way take up the kingdom for himself; [?as for] the captaincy*, despite what had been said and answered in the first discussion and afterwards, he said that His Excellency persisted *in the form and manner of the answer given these days to me, Sormano, which*, as said, I wrote in exactly that manner, *as irresolute and unclear* as it was given me. As for *making an agreement and settling his affairs with the [Pope]*, he confirmed what is said above. ### f. 122r Sire, from these discussions with this Lord Duke it seems one can conclude *that no great reliance should be placed on his really being willing to enter into or accept the captaincy, on which all the difficulties are put forward from His Excellency's side concerning provisions, circumstances and their dependencies*; and in our judgement, *taking the matter together with its provisions and dependencies so difficult, it seems that it is the difficulties, and not the will, that keep him from accepting; and this perhaps vain opinion of ours we did not think fit to keep from Your Majesty*. We will not fail to press His Excellency continually, and if we can obtain anything else from him it will be reported. I, Joachim, will wait here for the Lord Marshal Trivulzio, and we think that His Lordship, much esteemed by the said Lord Duke, will exert himself for this cause, which we are sure he will gladly do for the good of this business and Your Majesty's service. Ferrara, 23 February 1529. Written a few days after the 23 February pair, it reports the sequel of the agents' audiences with Alfonso d'Este. 2. The duke had already given "a not very clear and not resolute answer" on the captaincy (*capitaneato*) of the French army for the Naples enterprise; he has not accepted it, and the agents doubt he will. 3. Alfonso says he cannot see that the King and his confederates are making the provisions the enterprise needs — an army in the field, supplies, money for Swiss, Spaniards and Genoese — and that everything should be furnished before he commits. 4. Two things he asks the King to remember: the Naples enterprise, and (a second point around the captaincy) that he cannot take the command without the King's explicit provision. 5. He promises, from his side, not to fail; the agents say they have omitted nothing that was in their power. 6. Given the duke's nature, they judge the matter "not a little difficult", and put their hope in the authority and credit of the marshal Teodoro Trivulzio, expected in Ferrara on his way to Venice; de Vaulx will wait three or four days more for him. 7. The letter breaks off; its final leaf is not at f. 117. The catalogue listed it as a ciphered letter to an unknown recipient in London, 1516; it is a despatch in clear English except five lines on f. 40v. Where British Library, via four DECODE images; Unsolved Catalogue item 100. There is no contemporary decipherment. The cipher A substitution of invented signs with word division kept, plus a few word signs. How it was read A repeated nine-sign word fits “audensier”, spelled that way in clear on the same page, and gives the rest of the alphabet. Letters and Papers was checked only after the decipherment, and agrees. What it says The Audiencier and Luigi Marliano expect the King’s entry into Brussels at the end of the week, and the Emperor at Cambrai about the 15th. Credit Letters and Papers II no. 2862 (1864) already summarised the Cambrai clause, without the text or the Marliano and entry details. Still open Two word signs are identified only from context: the star is the Emperor, and one sign is probably the King. f. 40v: the cipher passage, after the clear words “and of this opinion is the”. spinelly1516.html#the-document

DECODE imaged four pages. In the order of the leaves they are P1 f. 40r, P3 f. 40v, P4 f. 41r and P2 f. 41v, which carries the end of the letter and the subscription “your most humble and … seruant Thommas Spynelly”. The dating clause reads “Written at Methlyn Bruxells the fyrst day of february M.D.XVJ”. The old foliation 33–34 is the one used by Letters and Papers . So DECODE’s place (London) and recipient (unknown) are wrong: the letter was written in Brussels to the King. The year is 1517. Spinelly was Henry’s resident agent in the Low Countries. The despatch reports the meetings of Maximilian and Charles with Chièvres, the Chancellor, the Audiencier and Hans Renner, the French embassy, and the cession of Verona to Lautrec under the treaty of Brussels. It also covers Cardinal Schiner’s anger at that cession and the Emperor’s intention to keep his amity with England.
spinelly1516.html#the-cipher

The cipher is a monoalphabetic substitution. Most signs are Greek or Latin letter forms given other values. Word division is kept, and a few signs stand for whole words. plain sign plain sign plain sign a φ i, y e r c b τ k λ s ʃ c 4 l triangle v; σ (?) t k d ʒ m y u (w = δδ) δ e o n b p q h ρ o 7 Word signs: ϑ = of ; ꝁ = this ; w with a bar = that ; a star with a superscript = the Emperor ; and a small sign after “the” at the end of line 2, probably the King .
spinelly1516.html#the-reading

The clear text runs into the cipher mid-sentence (“and of this opinion is the”): Audensier and misser Loys de Merlien. The whiche Audensier saythe that the [King] in the laterende of this wicke shall make his entree in to this town, and [the Emperor] about the xv day of the present monethe so to Cambray. The Audiencier is the head of Charles’s chancery secretariat, named only by office throughout the letter (probably Philippe Haneton). “Misser Loys de Merlien” is Luigi Marliano, Charles’s physician and councillor, later bishop of Tuy. The clear postscript on f. 41v, written after the King came back from Vilvoorde and the Emperor went back to Mechelen, says that the coming of “his magestye” into this town is put off because he “loke[th] for certeyn princes oute of Almayne, the which he wol have at his entree”. “His majesty” there may be the Emperor, which leaves open whose entry the cipher means (see section 05). The Emperor did go to Cambrai, where the treaty with France was signed on 11 March 1517.
spinelly1516.html#method

The nine-sign word φδʒobʃeoc occurs twice, and its fourth and eighth signs are the same. “Audensier”, spelled that way in clear two paragraphs above, fits the pattern. It gives a, u, d, e, n, s, i and r; φbʒ is then and . The frequent kρo is the , and k7 is to . The remaining values follow from the words they complete: present monethe , entree , town , and 4φyτcφe = Cambray . Every value except p and b occurs at least twice. Letters and Papers was checked only after the decipherment, and its summary (“about the 15th of this month the Emperor will go to Cambray”) agrees with it.
spinelly1516.html#what-remains-uncertain

The star sign = the Emperor: H, from context and the calendar. xbʒφe = “xv day”, with b written for the numeral v: H, from the calendar’s “15th”. The sign after “the” at the end of line 2 = the King: C. It is the subject of “make his entree” and sits against the gutter. The Emperor has his own sign later in the same sentence, which favours the King. σ as a second sign for l in “Loys”: C. The Audiencier as Philippe Haneton: C. With the uncertain signs above counted as holes, the 38-word passage reads at 92.7% of its words (measured 24 October 2026): coherent sentences, but under the 95% a complete reading needs.

I shall answer [it] orally [when I come?]. Since these matters may be of very great weight and bring great consequences: [here is my] answer to Your Honour’s request concerning passports here. Jealousy is beginning between the [106] and the [114] [105] envoys; both have left here. I know [113]’s whole intention, what he has in mind. Well, I have also kept a close watch on him. He has gone to the [114]. I rest neither night nor day, whether I am ill or not, and shrink from no danger. Contributor’s interpretation: the writer appears to be an agent or informant reporting to a superior. Passports, rivalry between envoys and their departure fit diplomatic activity, possibly a congress or mediation. The Swedish collection suggests a possible Swedish connection, and the references to 23 February and 13 March suggest writing later than the cited March letter. Late March or April is a working suggestion, not a recovered date. What was checked: the public DECODE record gives only the broad range 1600–1699, leaves the correspondents and languages blank, and still carries an unresolved catalogue status. Its general collection note concerns Oxenstierna correspondence, not an attribution of this specific letter. The supplied scan visibly carries a pencilled “1632?”. Neither this annotation nor archive custody proves the year or recipient. The earlier survey reports an Amsterdam address on another view; that view was checked on 18 October 2026 and does read Amsterdam (section 05). The earlier group survey records unsuccessful attacks on R4306 and tests of keys R4296/R4310. Note added 18 October 2026: that attempt (21 September 2026: simple and homophonic annealing over quadgram models in ten languages, Dutch among them, on two transcriptions; box keys R4310 and R4296 rejected) had its own entry from 14 October, which is now folded into this one; its transcriptions are kept in targets/sweden4306/project_attempt/ . No complete earlier plaintext was located in a limited opening-phrase search. No exhaustive publication search or first-publication claim is made. The identities of the four codes and the correspondents remain open.

Two despatches from Bonn, January and February 1759, in a numerical syllabary of 1759 with no surviving key. The key was recovered from the ciphertext alone, by a solver that keeps the table in alphabetical order, and corrected against the clear text around each run. 96% of the 553 groups decrypt; about 21 groups, mostly names, stay open. 290 312 343 429 288 291 150 337 429 312 405 337 la n ou ve l le c on ve n ti on alphabetical table · a 100 · de 180 · la 290 · pr 357 · t 398 · z 442 Bonn → Brussels · numerical syllabary · January–February 1759 · key recovered from ciphertext-only Gottfried van Swieten to Count Cobenzl, Bonn 1759 from Gottfried van Swieten → to Count Cobenzl Go to the full text ↓ Two reports on the French armies in Germany, in a numbered syllabary with no surviving key; the key was recovered from the ciphertext alone and 96% of the 553 groups decrypt. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: complete · On the map ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · complete The letters Gottfried van Swieten, the Empress’s diplomat at the Elector of Cologne’s court in Bonn, to Count Cobenzl, minister plenipotentiary at Brussels, 14 January and 4 February 1759. Where Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État et de Guerre inv. 1236, ff. 327–328 and 344–345; DECODE R957 and R956, listed as not decrypted. The cipher Three-digit numbers 100–442 for letters, syllables and a few words, in alphabetical order with occasional second numbers; unseparated runs inside clear French. How it was decrypted An annealer that keeps the table in alphabetical order, scored by a French language model, broke it on one start in eight; the rest was corrected against the clear text around each run. What it says The convention that left Prussian Gueldre’s revenues to the French, Moers handed to a prince without asking the Empress, and Soubise’s army living on contributions with only Broglie competent among its generals. Still open Two name groups in the letter of 4 February, each seen once. The reading audit of 22 October 2026 had set the letter of 14 January back to decoded, not read (two of its four sentences did not build); its contemporary decipherment, found on the DECODE record the next day, settles them. This page was split on 14 October 2026 from the joint page for van Swieten’s three letters. The undated letter of 1757–58 uses an earlier table, and its decipherment is written under it, a different cipher with its own page: Van Swieten to Cobenzl, 1757–58 .

Record Folio, date Cipher Decrypted R957 ff. 327–328, Bonn, 14 January 1759 210 groups in two unbroken runs all but four groups R956 ff. 344–345, Bonn, 4 February 1759 343 groups in nineteen runs set inside clear sentences all but about 16 groups In 1759 the digits run on with no separators. They divide into threes, which the lengths of the runs confirm. Four DECODE transcriptions had dropped or doubled digits; those runs were transcribed again from the scans.
swieten1759.html#method

The 1759 numbers do not fit the 1757 values of the earlier letter , but if the new table was built the same way, it has a strong constraint: a higher number never stands for an alphabetically earlier syllable. The solver ( msolve.py ) keeps one inventory index per observed number, sorted, and allows at most two numbers per syllable. It anneals the boundaries against a French character model ( fr-1750-nospace , added to the shared lang/ registry), with a small bonus per decoded letter. As a control, a 274-group French passage encoded with a random alphabetical table was recovered verbatim. On the real 491 clean groups, one start in eight gave “la nouvelle convention on laisse le revenu… en réservant la souveraineté… l’impératrice”, and the other seven did not. The key was then corrected by hand, run by run, against the French sentence each run sits in. For example, “avant que les campagnes soient garnies, on ne songe pas à faire des magazins , si ce n’est aux dépens des États de l’Empire qui sont entièrement épuisés”. The end of the table falls into place: x 438/439, y 441, z 442. So do word entries filed in their alphabetical slot: nous, pour, qui, roi, comte. R956, f. 344: runs of unseparated digits inside the clear text (“le grand principe paroît être de faire 392 135 133 389 385 403…” = subsister l’armée du roi y sans qu’il en coûte un sou ). Image: Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État et de Guerre inv. 1236 f. 344, via DECODE R956.
swieten1759.html#r957

The fourth DECODE image of R957, never opened before, is a contemporary decipherment of this passage on a separate leaf in another hand; the decipherer wrote 232 above France . Aligned group by group with the figures (23 October 2026), it agrees word for word once seven values of the table rebuilt here are corrected, each at every occurrence: 232 France , 327 oc , 131 ay , 170 cr , 323 o , 440 y , 316 ni ; 327 and 440 close two of the table’s order breaks. One group is the encipherer’s slip (357 pr for -on in supposition ). The table was rebuilt from the ciphertext before the decipherment was seen; the decipherment now confirms it. The passage ( R957_reading.md , English R957_en.md ): … de l’administration; la nouvelle Convention laisse les Revenus à la France en reservant la Souveraineté à l’Imperatrice. On procede toujours de la part des français dans cette Supposition, sans que nous ayons aucun ordre de la Cour a ce sujet; cela cause beaucoups de mesintelligences. On vient de la part de la france de mettre en possession de la principauté de Moeurs le Prince de Croÿ, qui y forme des pretensions, sans prevenir seulement l’Imperatrice, qui en est souveraine. The September decode had “On promet de toujours”, “la [G…]” and “le prince de Con[…] […] qui vous formez” at these places. The Prussian lands on the Lower Rhine (Gueldre, Moers) were in French and Austrian hands from 1757. The passage records a convention that left their revenues to one party and the sovereignty to Maria Theresa. It also reports that the French have put the Prince of Croÿ in possession of Moers, which he claimed, without informing her. The corrected values also give two names in the letter of 4 February: Crillon and Dumenil .
swieten1759.html#r956

Il est constant que l’armée du Prince de Soubise est dans le meilleur état qu’on puisse imaginer … avant que les campagnes soient garnies, on ne songe pas à faire des magazins si ce n’est aux dépens des États de l’Empire qui sont entièrement épuisés; le grand principe paraît être de faire subsister l’armée du roi y sans qu’il en coûte un sou . La campagne passée en fait la preuve, aussi le prince [name] a-t-il avoué que les contributions de la Gueldre avoient suffi à l’entretien de son armée , et qu’on avoit même transmis assez d’argent à l’armée de Contades pour subvenir aux frais du traitement des troupes pendant l’hiver , et que toutes les opérations de l’année passée n’avoient eu d’autre but. Le prince pense bien, mais le reste est malintentionné ; outre cela il n’y a pas un officier général entendu à cette armée, excepté le duc de Broglio; le m[aréchal] général des logis de Vaut est intéressé et ignorant, et non l’intendant nécessaire pour mettre en œuvre le système que j’ai détaillé ci-dessus … D’ailleurs, homme non violent , je n’ai pas besoin de parler de Dumesnil ; il est universellement connu pour être prussien, […] le prince Camille … Parmi les maréchaux de ce[…] il n’y a que [name] qu’on estime . Comme de notre côté nous ne pouvons pas résister aux plaintes fondées des États , et que les ordres de la cour nous obligent de faire des représentations … on a pris occasion de former des plaintes contre le comte de Pergen comme s’il n’agissoit pas conformément aux intérêts de la cause commune.
swieten1759.html#residuals

232 (twice, R957): France , from the contemporary decipherment (23 October 2026); it had been left open as a name filed under G. 147 100 126 148 (R956): the prince who “avowed”. From the context it should be Soubise, but the numbers are out of alphabetical order, so this is probably a name group. Not decrypted (I). 170 323 441 (R957) is Croÿ and 170 271 289 337 (R956) Crillon , once 170 = cr and 323 = o were corrected from the decipherment of R957. 290 313 316 313 373 (R956): the one marshal “qu’on estime”. The syllables decrypt to la-n-ne-n-r and the name is not identified; the digit division here is uncertain in the scan. Not decrypted (I). R957’s awkward “on promet de toujours” is On procede toujours in the decipherment; the pr in supposition is the encipherer’s slip. 300 and 294 238 (R956): “le m[aréchal] général des logis de Vaut”. Each number occurs only once, and its value comes from its place in the alphabetical table (I). 300 lies between 299 ma and 303 me , so it is mar… or a word entry such as maréchal rather than m . 294 comes after 293 li and can be lo ; 238 comes before 239 g and can be a second g ; with 281 is they give logis . The earlier reading here, “le major général des Liégeois”, needed 238 = ge , a ge placed before g (239) and ga (240), and its letters do not spell Liégeois. The maréchal général des logis ran the marches and quarters of a French army. The officer is probably François-Eugène de Vault (1717–1790): a memorandum by “M. de Vault” on the armies in Germany, August 1758, is filed with Soubise’s campaign papers. His post in 1759 has not been verified (I).

La campagne passée en fait la preuve, aussi «le prince [147 100 126 148]» a-t-il avoué que les «contributions de la Gueldre» avoient «suffi à l'entretien de son armée» et qu'on avoit même «transmis assez d'argent à l'armée de Contades» pour subvenir aux frais «du traitement des troupes pendant l'hiver», et que toutes les opérations de l'année passée n'avoient «eu d'autre but. Le prince pense» bien, mais le reste est «malintentionné»; outre cela «il n'y a pas un officier général entendu à cette armée, excepté le duc de Broglio; le m[aréchal] (I) général des logis (I) de Vaut est intéressé et ignorant, et non l'intendant nécessaire pour mettre en oeuvre le système» que j'ai détaillé ci-dessus, sans s'oublier quant à ses intérêts propres, auxquels il est fort attaché. D'ailleurs, «homme non violent», je n'ai pas besoin de «parler de Dumenil»; il est universellement connu pour être «prussien, Crillon (170 271 289 337, read 23 Oct 2026 with 170 = cr from R957), le prince Camille (?)» plusieurs bien, mais c'est à quoi se borne tout ce qu'ils peuvent faire de bon pour la cause commune. Parmi «les maréchaux de ce[…]» il n'y a que «[290 313 316 313 373] qu'on estime». Comme de notre côté nous ne pouvons pas résister aux «plaintes fondées des États», et que «les ordres de la cour» nous obligent de faire des représentations … on a pris occasion de former des plaintes contre «le comte de Pergen» comme s'il n'agissoit pas conformément aux intérêts de la cause commune … (I) = inferred from the number's place in the alphabetical table and the sense (corrected 30 Sept 2026; first read "le major (?) général des Liégeois"): 291 300 241 315 375 289 181 294 238 281 180 428 420 399 = le m[aréchal] général des lo-g-is de Vaut. 300 lies between 299 ma and 303 me (mar… or a word entry maréchal rather than m); 294 after 293 li (lo); 238 before 239 g (a second g; "ge" would stand ahead of g and of 240 ga, 241 ge). Each number occurs once. The officer is probably François-Eugène de Vault (1717-1790); his post in 1759 is not verified. An excerpt. --> # R956, Gottfried van Swieten to Count Cobenzl, Bonn, 4 February 1759 (ff. 344-345): English translation It is certain that the Prince de Soubise's army is in the best state imaginable … before the countryside is stocked, «no one is thinking of making magazines» except «at the expense of the Estates of the Empire, which» are entirely exhausted; the great principle seems to be to make «the King's army subsist there without its costing a sou». The past campaign is proof of it; and so «the prince [147 100 126 148]» admitted that the «contributions of Guelders» had «sufficed for the upkeep of his army» and that enough money had even been «sent to Contades's army» to meet the costs «of the troops' pay during the winter», and that all the operations of the past year had «had no other aim. The prince thinks» well, but the rest are «ill-intentioned»; besides that, «there is not one capable general officer in this army except the Duc de Broglie; the m[arshal] (I) general of the quarters (I), de Vaut, is self-interested and ignorant, and not the intendant needed to put into practice the system» that I have detailed above, without forgetting himself as to his own interests, to which he is much attached. Moreover, «a man not violent», I have no need to «speak of Dumenil»; he is universally known to be «Prussian; Crillon, the Prince Camille (?)» several good, but that is the limit of all the good they can do for the common cause. Among «the marshals of th[…]» there is only «[290 313 316 313 373] who is esteemed». As on our side we cannot resist «the well-founded complaints of the Estates», and «the orders of the court» oblige us to make representations … occasion has been taken to make complaints against «the Count of Pergen», as if he were not acting in accordance with the interests of the common cause … Key: key.json

Three letters wholly in a nomenclator of homophones and three-letter code groups. The key was recovered by aligning two sibling letters with the clerk’s decipherment filed after them, then applied to the three; 96.5% of their tokens have a value. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 18 September 2026 · updated 5 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial (49% of the cipher) · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial (49% of the cipher) The letters Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, his ambassador at Rome: N.45 (Seville, 4 April 1511), N.57 (Burgos, 5 June 1512) and N.60 (Logroño, 1 September 1512), the three of 1511–12 filed without a clerk’s decipherment. Where Archivo Histórico Nacional, Vich family papers, Estado legajos 8714 and 8715. The cipher A nomenclator: a homophonic alphabet of figures and marked letters, and about 150 three-letter code groups for whole words ( pef que , mix papa ) and for syllables inside spelt-out words. How it was read Lining up two deciphered siblings with their decipherments gave the alphabet and the common groups; the three cipher-only letters were then deciphered with it. What it says N.45 complains of Julius II, who published new cardinals and absolved the Venetians without consulting Ferdinand. N.57 is Ferdinand’s account of how his army was pushed into the battle of Ravenna against his orders. N.60 sets out the restoration of Massimiliano Sforza in Milan and resists the Pope’s claims to Parma, Piacenza, Modena and Reggio. Still open By the notes’ estimate about 5, 7 and 14 per cent of the text of N.45, N.57 and N.60 is without a value or doubtful. N.73 (1515) is not deciphered. The Barón de Terrateig’s 1963 edition was not seen; the letters may already be printed there.

Jerónimo de Vich, a Valencian noble, was Ferdinand’s ambassador at Rome through the pontificate of Julius II and into that of Leo X. His family’s papers passed to the Archivo Histórico Nacional and are catalogued with the Estado section, legajos 8714 and 8715. A PARES search for Vich cifrada lists the ciphered items. Most of them have a contemporary decipherment on the leaves that follow the cipher, written out in clear by a clerk at Rome; three of 1511–12 do not, and neither does one of 1515, which is in another cipher and has its own page . Signature Date Place State 8714 N.12 30 Sept 1508 cipher and decipherment 8714 N.26 28 July 1509 cipher and decipherment 8714 N.39 13 May 1510 Monzón cipher and decipherment 8715 N.41 22 May 1510 cipher and decipherment; same key as below 8715 N.45 4 Apr 1511 Seville cipher only — deciphered here, 89.3% of words read 8715 N.46 5 July 1511 cipher and decipherment — key source 8715 N.52BIS 1 Mar 1512 cipher and decipherment — key source 8715 N.57 5 June 1512 Burgos cipher only — deciphered here, 92.8% of words read 8715 N.60 1 Sept 1512 Logroño cipher only — decoded here, not read 8715 N.73 26 Oct 1515 Pedrezuela cipher only; a different system, not deciphered ( own page ) 8715 N.74 30 Jan 1519 Charles I; cipher and decipherment in a third system 8715 N.79 “1500” “Clave de cifra”: a plain letter-to-sign table, not the key to any of these The letters are long. N.45 runs to thirteen pages of cipher (378 lines), N.60 to thirteen (432 lines), N.57 to one page and three lines. Apart from the heading date, the closing dateline and the royal signature, everything is in cipher. N.46, 5 July 1511: the first lines of the cipher (above) and of the clerk’s decipherment filed after it (below), Con beltran de cordona que partio de Sevilla a xvj de junio respondi a vuestras letras y scrivi todo lo que mas me ocorria; despues no he recebido vuestras … In the cipher, sal has pef is todo lo que , fid despues , mik no , par recebido , sub vuestras . Pairs like this gave the key. Image: Archivo Histórico Nacional, Estado 8715 N.46, images 1 and 3, via PARES; the two strips set together here.

One key serves N.41, N.45, N.46, N.52BIS, N.57 and N.60, from May 1510 to September 1512. It has two parts. A homophonic alphabet. Each letter is written with one to three signs: figures, and letters with bars, loops or dots added. The labels below are the ASCII names used in the transcriptions, not the shapes themselves. letter signs letter signs letter signs a to 7 b h O p P SS mt b B i e Z r 40 tt E c ch l c s d eh d oo ll 7o t X g 9 e 4h 3 m q u 3t f gh n 11 W v V g o o ah T y / z 8 / p Code groups. Lowercase groups of two to five letters, most of three, stand for words: pef que , diz de , dih con , fak el , hor la , has lo , raf por , rif porque , mix and mye papa , fef emperador , sap venecianos , fio Ferrara , fuq Francia , dur / dox / dux duque , hib guerra , gup batalla , mak Nápoles , hel Ingalaterra . Some are syllables used inside words that are otherwise spelt out: pob si in si-t-io , flart me in pri-me-ras , mik no in me-no-r , plort al in c-al-dero . The groups are not in alphabetical order of their meanings, but related words often share an initial: f for el, en, es, esta, estado, emperador, Ferrara, Francia, franceses , m for mucho, muy, mil, manera, Nápoles, no, nos , p and r for que, quiere, quales, por, para, parte . Several words have two or three groups. In all 153 groups have been recovered; the full list is in targets/vich1511/key.md . Traps. fug is señor and fuq Francia , and the two differ by a tail. plart mi and plort al differ by one letter, and the transcribers of N.45 and N.60 read the second differently; its value al is supported by c- plort -dero in N.57. The barred q is m in most places and a in a few: on the leaf there seem to be two similar signs, m with two bars and a with one, which the transcription has merged. In N.60 a tailed 8 reads i / j , and P serves for j and y as well as p .
vich1511.html#method

No part of the key was recovered from the ciphertext alone. N.46 (5 July 1511) and N.52BIS (1 March 1512) are in the same key and each has the clerk’s decipherment on the leaves after the cipher. Both were transcribed sign by sign from the PARES images, and the cipher was lined up with the decipherment word by word, as in the figure above. That gave the alphabet and the commoner code groups. The three cipher-only letters were then transcribed in the same labels and decoded by script ( decode.py ). Where the decode left a group without a value, its value was fixed from the sense of the surrounding Spanish and accepted only when it gave sense elsewhere too; fio Ferrara , dur duque , fuq Francia , gib franceses and sum tierra were added this way. The key went from the groups the two siblings supply to 153.
vich1511.html#check

Built on two letters, applied to three others. The alphabet and the core groups come from N.46 and N.52BIS alone. Applied to N.45, N.57 and N.60, which contributed nothing to them, they give running Spanish. The datelines. Each letter’s place and date are written in clear at the foot, and they agree with the catalogue: Seville, Burgos, Logroño. The contents fit the dates. N.45 complains of Julius II’s publication of new cardinals, which fits the promotion of 10 March 1511, less than four weeks earlier. N.57 turns on a battle lost after the Pope’s side and Vich pressed the viceroy to fight, which fits Ravenna (11 April 1512). N.60 starts from bulas para lo de [?Navarra] and puts Massimiliano Sforza into Milan, which fits the Navarre campaign of summer 1512 and the Sforza restoration agreed that August. None of this is in the clear text. A proverb spelt out. In N.57, echar la soga tras el caldero (to throw the rope after the bucket) is spelt out sign by sign except for el , and for al in c-al-dero , which are code groups. A spelt-out proverb that comes out right is hard to get by accident. N.57, lines 26–28: … que seria ec- / -har la soga tras el caldero. Lo que en este caso de la / guerra toca hazer a vos … es procurar que el papa y venecianos cumplan . On the middle line, hor is la , fak el , and plort the al of caldero ; on the last, hib guerra , mix papa , sap venecianos . Image: Archivo Histórico Nacional, Estado 8715 N.57, image 1, via PARES. N.57, the end: the last three lines of cipher ( … y la de Ferrara … que la trateys … sin que la sienta el papa … hazedme lo saber ), the dateline in clear, en burgos a v de junio de dxij , and the royal signature. Quotations are from the readings of 22–23 October 2026 ( n45_reading.md , n57_reading.md , n60_reading.md , with English in _en.md ), in the figures’ own 1511 spelling; [..] marks groups without a value, [?word] a word the figures carry only in part A long complaint against Julius II, then instructions. It opens with the news Vich had sent: the publication of the new cardinals, la publicacion de los nueve cardenales que crio el papa , which Ferdinand takes as proof that the Pope will not follow his counsel. The Pope has absolved the Venetians and treated with them sin dezirme ni comunicarme ; he has not kept his promise over the priory of San Juan; and because he would not follow Ferdinand’s advice to keep his army out of danger, there followed la rota que dezis . The business is the Emperor and Venice. Ferdinand gives draft terms for their concord: Padua and Treviso to stay with Venice in fief against a tribute, Verona, Vicenza, Riva, Rovereto and Peschiera to go to the Emperor; Yo estoy muy determinado de ser perpetuamente unido con el emperador . France is offering him a separate perpetual alliance without the Emperor, which he will not take, and a rupture would wreck his war against the Moors. Orders go to Fabrizio Colonna under an enclosed letter of credence. Near the end he sums up the three points Vich is to press: La primera, que la gente del papa este en lugar seguro y donde no se aventure … La segunda, que apreteys muy [..]te la conclusion de la concordia del emperador y de los venecianos. Y la tercera, la concordia de Ferrara; todo esto de la manera que de suso [..] dicho. “First, that the Pope’s troops stay in a safe place where they are not put at risk; second, that you press very hard for the conclusion of the concord between the Emperor and the Venetians; and third, the settlement of Ferrara, all in the way set out above.”

The aftermath of Ravenna, where on 11 April 1512 the French destroyed the army of the Holy League under Ferdinand’s viceroy of Naples, Ramón de Cardona. Ferdinand reconstructs how his army came to fight. Vich’s letters, and the papal side, pressed the viceroy, saying que si no la hazian el papa no compliria la paga y que se concertaria con Francia , if they did not fight the Pope would not meet the pay and would come to terms with France; and this against Ferdinand’s repeated written orders not to risk a battle. tened por cierto que las cosas de guerra es muy [?peligroso] […] governar los que estan absentes dellas, que siempre se ha de remitir a los que las tienen presentes “Be sure that in matters of war it is very dangerous for those who are absent from them to govern them; they must always be left to those who have them in front of them.” Do not do it again, he says, for it would be echar la soga tras el caldero , to lose the rope after the bucket. What is left to Vich is to procurar que el papa y venecianos cumplan their share of the pay, to bring the Emperor’s business to a conclusion, and to treat the Ferrara business secretly, sin que la sienta el papa , and report back, que yo dare orden como se efectue .

Written from the Navarre campaign, the longest and least complete of the three, and decoded, not read : proofread sign by sign on 23 October 2026 (140 label corrections, chiefly an inverted T for o transcribed as t about a hundred times, and four new group values: poh quanto, fub dan, ror parece, soi tanto), it still has holes in too many sentences, from about 600 groups ( phi 34 times, reg 18, pub 14 …) that occur in no deciphered sibling. The quotations below are from its partial reading. Its parts, in order: Reproach to Julius II (pp. 3–5). Vich had sent the bulas para lo de [?Navarra] , and word that the Pope was acting against what had been agreed. Ferdinand recites what he has spent por tierra y por mar to rescue the Pope, the Church and Italy, and the Pope’s ingratitude in not paying his troops as the League requires. He traces it to the Pope’s suspicion que el Emperador y yo nos [..] apoderar de Italia, no siendo assi la [?verdad] (“mean to seize Italy”), and tells Vich to remove it. Milan (pp. 6–8). The Emperor and Ferdinand agree that Massimiliano, fijo del duque Ludouico , be put into the duchy by the Emperor’s hand, so that Pope and Venice lose the suspicion that Milan is being taken for the Emperor; possession of the state and its fortresses is to be taken at once in Massimiliano’s name. A marriage is in view for el infante don [?Fernando] , Ferdinand’s grandson, with la fija de la duquesa de Milan . Venice and the papal claims (p. 9). Venice should not be stopped from recovering the towns it held before the war, or it will not pay. The Pope is trying to take Parma, Piacenza, Modena and Reggio, against the capitulation of the League, under which no member is to act en perjuyzio de otra ; that is to wait until Milan is secured. Spiritual war on Louis XII (pp. 10–11). Ferdinand wants the Pope to use las armas espirituales : to deprive the King of France of his crown and of Guyenne and Normandy, as principal fautor y receptador [..] cismaticos y hereticos , to absolve his subjects of obedience and grant a crusade against him, as was done against the Emperor Frederick and King Pedro. Money, and Milan before Ferrara (pp. 12–15). Pensions of cinquenta mil ducados de pension cada año , shared among the members of the League, to hold an Italian power to it, que es muy sustancial ; if the Pope insists on beginning with Ferrara, Vich is to insist on finishing the French in the state of Milan first, and on a mutual guarantee of each member’s state in Italy.

Possibly. The Barón de Terrateig, Política en Italia del Rey Católico 1507–1516. Correspondencia inédita con el embajador Vich (CSIC, Madrid 1963, 2 vols.), edits this correspondence, and it was not seen for this work. What could be found out about it without the book (web searches and Google Books snippets, 18 September 2026): Volume II prints Ferdinand’s letters to Vich as numbered documents with AHN Estado references; a snippet shows a letter dated Logroño a XXVI días de octubre 1512 followed by Documento n.° 89, A.H.N. Estado , and later historians cite 1512 letters in vol. II from p. 206 on. The book has plates of ciphered letters and prints Descifrado de la carta que figura en la lámina … beside them, and its index has many entries under Rávena, batalla de . No snippet, review or citation was found that quotes or cites the letters of 4 April 1511, 5 June 1512 or 1 September 1512, or says whether Terrateig printed cipher-only letters in clear. So it is open whether Terrateig printed N.45, N.57 and N.60, and if so whether he printed a decipherment of them. Given that his volume II prints Ferdinand’s 1512 letters from this legajo, it should be assumed until checked that he may have. PARES itself records no decipherment for these three items.

The notes put the share of text still without sense or doubtful higher, about 5, 7 and 14 %, because some stretches decode letter by letter without yet making sense. The other deciphered letters in the same key (N.41, 8714 N.39 and N.12) were aligned on 5 October and added about 85 groups; N.60’s open groups gz , phi , reg , goi and sid occur in none of them. Look-alike signs. The q sign for m and a , and the group pairs plart / plort and flart / flort , need one careful pass against the images before they are trusted. Single-context values. Some groups were fixed from one or two contexts in the three letters. fer , for instance, is keyed as dio(s) , but it also stands where Fer- of Fernando is wanted; it may be a syllable group, not a word. N.60, decoded, not read. About 600 groups without a value ( phi 34 times, reg 18, pub 14, and many seen once), none of them in a deciphered sibling, so they need a value that fits every occurrence or another decipherment; a few signs under ink blots and paper holes, and a few short strokes at the limit of the PARES images. In N.45 and N.57, about 424 and 24 short holes stay, on groups that occur in no deciphered sibling. goi ( aquel ) and sid ( son ) were valued on 22 October 2026; gz is a clause mark. With these holes N.45 reads at 89.3% of its words and N.57 at 92.8% (measured 24 October 2026): both build coherent sentences, but under the 95% a complete reading needs. Readings from sense. In N.60, the word after que el Emperador y yo nos has no value; apoderar follows it. Guyenne and Normandy are in the decode, but whom they are to go to sits in groups without a value; the notes’ “assigned to England” is an inference. The duquesa de Milan whose daughter is proposed for the infante is presumably Isabella of Aragon, widow of Gian Galeazzo Sforza, and the daughter Bona; the decipherment does not name them. A nearby line reads el fijo del duque Ludovico que mato a su padre , whose sense in context is not settled. Prior publication. See section 08. The three letters may already be in print in Terrateig 1963, which was not consulted.

And given how earnestly you wrote to me before the battle that on no account was it fitting that they should [?retire], [..] [..] said that I have [..] written so to my viceroy, I know that they speak the truth; and that the fear you had, those of you who were in Rome, and the things you wrote from there to our camp [and] captain general, made those who were with him pervert the whole order of war; for the truth is that everything [..] [..] from the beginning to the end was [?mistaken], and against all order of war. And they say that [..] they were pressed by you to do so, because at every one of these points you told them that if they did not do it [i.e. fight] the Pope would not pay his share and would come to terms with France; and on the other hand, in the end, you wrote to them so firmly that Rome would be [..] if they withdrew, that these things pressed them into putting themselves in the [..] and disadvantage into which they put themselves, even though they did not do what I had sent to tell them; for it is clear that not withdrawing could not be squared with what you wrote to them: [..] to place themselves where they would not come to battle, which is what I [..] them, knowing that in this lay the [..], because the [?one] is [..] on the other. And take it for certain that in matters of war it is very [?dangerous] [..] for those who are absent from them to govern them; they must always be left to those who have them in front of them [..] any. And I say all this so that from now on you take great care not to fall into such [?an error], for that would be throwing the rope after the bucket. What it falls to you to do in this matter of the war [..] is to get the Pope and the Venetians to fulfil [..] the pay that they are bound to by the League, and to negotiate very well the [..] [..], and the conclusion of the Emperor's business and all the other negotiations that [..] for the good of the enterprise. From the 1720s the Deciphering Branch in London broke the ciphers of intercepted foreign letters. It kept each key it rebuilt, and many of those keys are now bound in the British Library’s Additional Manuscripts. Add MS 32270 holds the keys for the German courts and for the Empire: Palm, Kinsky and Wasner for Vienna, then Bavaria, Brunswick, Hesse-Kassel and the Palatinate. Folio 42 sits among the imperial keys. The endorsement dates it to 1727 and names the parties. “Here” is London, where the branch worked. The table is headed by the ministers whose names a Brussels–London correspondence needed in 1727: Walpole, Townshend, Sinzendorff (the imperial chancellor), Staremberg, Richelieu. The places it names are Ostenda, Ollanda, Annover and Parigi. The words include Commercio, Trattato, Congresso and Pace. Together they point to the dispute over the Ostend Company and the congress that followed it. The table is the branch’s reconstruction of the key. About a hundred of the 300 places are empty; 262–300 are blank. Some values have a dotted underline, which marks a doubtful value (Governo, Rialso, progetto, Camara bassa, Arciduchessa). Three places are guesses, written “p.n. of a country”, “p.n. of a place (Londra)” and “p.n. of a Place (Amsterdam)”. At 172 Imperadore is struck out because it was already at 218. These marks show a key recovered from intercepted letters.
